templates.description: Implements CT.DM-P10: Stakeholder privacy preferences are included in algorithmic design objectives and outputs are evaluated against these preferences.
templates.objective: To ensure the privacy preferences of the people affected by an automated decision are written into its design objectives and that what it produces is judged against them.
templates.successCriteria:
Every automated decision in scope names the stakeholder groups whose privacy preferences bind it, and each excluded model carries a reason and the person who agreed it.
The design objectives of each in-scope algorithm state the privacy preferences they are built to honour.
Outputs produced during the period have been examined against those preferences, not only against the model specification.
Each divergence between an output and a stated preference has a decision recorded against it.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the scope list of automated decisions with the stakeholder groups attached to each.
Collect the design objective documents showing the privacy preferences built into each in-scope algorithm.
Gather the exclusions recorded for models kept out of scope, with the reason and the person who agreed.
Retrieve the comparison notes covering the outputs examined during the period.
Obtain a sample of actual algorithm outputs from the same period.

Analysis:
Verify that each stakeholder group's stated preferences are traceable into a design objective rather than into a general policy statement.
Test the sampled outputs against the preferences recorded for that algorithm and check whether the comparison note reached the same result.
Examine whether each exclusion rests on a recorded reason and an identified approver.
Assess the disposition recorded against each divergence and whether the model or its objectives changed as a result.

Output:
A mapping of automated decisions to stakeholder groups and the preferences bound to each.
Findings from the assessor's own re-test of sampled outputs against the stated preferences.
A list of divergences with their recorded decisions and any left unresolved.

title.en: Settle which automated decisions fall in scope and whose privacy preferences bind them

description.en: List the automated decisions and inferences this control covers, and against each one the groups whose privacy preferences its design objectives must answer to. Those groups run wider than the people whose data trains or feeds the model: the individuals the outputs are applied to hold preferences as well, and many will never have touched the system. Where a model is left out, record the reason and the person who agreed it, so the omission can be argued with later rather than discovered.

evidenceHint.en: Scope list of the automated decisions covered, the stakeholder groups attached to each, and every model excluded with its reason and the person who agreed.

title.en: Record the privacy preferences built into algorithmic design objectives

description.en: Where processing produces automated decisions or inferences, record the privacy preferences stakeholders hold, how each was turned into a design objective, and how the outputs were compared against those objectives. Record the comparisons that failed as well as those that passed, with what changed as a result.

title.en: Examine what each algorithm produced against the preferences its objectives carry

description.en: Pull the outputs a model actually produced over the period and hold each recorded preference up against them, rather than re-reading the design note that states it. A model retrained on fresher data can drift away from a preference its objectives still claim, and the objective itself will not announce the drift. Record every divergence found together with the decision taken on it: the model changed, its use narrowed, or the divergence accepted and why. Accepted divergences written down as plainly as corrected ones are what let the next reader tell an honoured preference from a quietly abandoned one.

evidenceHint.en: Comparison note naming the period and the outputs examined, each preference tested against them, every divergence found, and the decision recorded on each.

templates.title: Limiting observability and linkability
templates.description: Implements CT.DP-P1: Data are processed to limit observability and linkability (e.g., data actions take place on local devices, privacy-preserving cryptography).
templates.objective: To ensure data actions are carried out so that fewer parties can observe them and the data they leave behind cannot readily be joined back to the individual it concerns.
templates.successCriteria:
Each data action carries a recorded disassociation technique and states where the processing physically happens.
Relinkage attempts have been made on disassociated data sets using available material, with the outcome and any residual identification recorded.
The parties able to observe each data action are known, and any widening since the last review was accepted by a named owner.
The holdings a data set could be matched against are listed and revisited as new sources appear.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the record of disassociation applied to each data action, naming the technique and where processing takes place.
Collect the relinkage test records showing the data set attacked, the material used in the attempt and the outcome.
Gather the review note listing, per data action, the parties holding visibility today.
Retrieve the list of internal and external holdings the data set could be matched against.

Analysis:
Re-perform a relinkage attempt on one disassociated data set using only material an ordinary insider could reach.
Compare the observers recorded for each data action with the access actually granted on the systems carrying it.
Check whether newly available holdings were added to the matchable list and the linkability judgement revisited.
Assess whether residual identification found in testing led to a change or was accepted on the record.

Output:
A statement of the disassociation in force per data action with the technique named.
The result of the assessor's own relinkage attempt, including any identifier recovered.
A table of observers per data action with every unapproved widening marked.

title.en: Record the disassociation applied to each data action so identified

description.en: For every action marked as not needing full identification, record what is actually done to limit identification, linkage or observability, and what identifying material still remains after it. The remaining material is the part a later re-association test is aimed at, so record it precisely rather than as a reassurance.

title.en: Test whether a disassociated data set can be linked back to an individual

description.en: Take a data set the organisation treats as disassociated and attempt, using material the organisation itself holds or could obtain, to link it back to a person. Record what was achievable, what was not, and what the attempt reveals about the residual recorded earlier.

evidenceHint.en: Test record naming the data set, the material used in the attempt, the outcome, and the residual identification found.

title.en: Revisit who can watch each data action and what it can now be joined against

description.en: Observability widens quietly: an action that once ran on the user's own device is moved to a shared service, a log gains a new reader, a feed acquires an intermediary, and a newly arrived data set makes two previously separate records matchable. For each action the organisation treats as limited, name every party that can see it take place today and every holding it could be matched against, then set that beside the position recorded when the limitation was put in. Where either has widened, state whether an owner accepted the widening or it simply happened unnoticed.

evidenceHint.en: Review note listing, per action, the parties with visibility today, the holdings it could be matched against, and whether any widening was accepted by a named owner.

templates.title: Limiting identification of individuals
templates.description: Implements CT.DP-P2: Data are processed to limit the identification of individuals (e.g., de-identification privacy techniques, tokenization).
templates.objective: To ensure an individual is no more identifiable within a data set than its purpose actually requires, with identifying detail dropped, coarsened or held back.
templates.successCriteria:
Data actions that do not need an identifiable individual are marked as such, and those that do carry the purpose making identification necessary.
Each treated data set has a recorded transformation naming the fields dropped, the values coarsened or banded, and the records held back.
A before-and-after extract exists for a treated data set, showing the identifying detail that is no longer present.
Identification still retained has been re-tested against the purpose now relied on.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the list of data actions with the identifiability each one requires.
Collect the transformation record per treated data set, naming fields dropped, values coarsened or banded and records held back.
Gather the before-and-after extract kept for at least one treated data set.
Retrieve the review list pairing the identification retained with the purpose relied on.

Analysis:
Query a treated data set directly and confirm the suppressed and generalised attributes are absent from the stored values, not merely hidden at the presentation layer.
Compare the band widths and groupings actually present in the data against those named in the transformation record.
Test whether an attribute recorded as dropped survives in an index, an export or a backup copy of the same data set.
Assess each retained identifier against its stated purpose and note where a reduction was raised but never made.

Output:
A data-action list annotated with required identifiability against the identifiability observed.
Verification results per treated data set, naming any attribute found that should have been removed.
A schedule of retained identification with its purpose and the reduction decisions outstanding.

title.en: Identify the data actions where individuals need not remain identifiable

description.en: Go through the processing map and judge, per data action, whether its purpose can be met without identifying the individual, without records being linkable to each other, or without the processing being observable to other parties. Record the judgement and the reason on each action, including the actions judged to need full identification.

title.en: Generalise or suppress the attributes that still identify an individual

description.en: Work through the actions marked as not needing an identifiable individual and change the data itself: coarsen dates and locations, band small counts, drop the direct identifiers, and hold back the rare combinations only a handful of records share. Stripping name and account number rarely finishes the job — a postcode, a birth date and a job title together will name someone in a small population, so the question is whether any record still stands alone after the transformation, not whether the obvious fields are gone. Run the transformation where the data enters the non-identifying use rather than as a later pass over a copy, or the identifiable original keeps feeding whatever reads it.

evidenceHint.en: The transformation applied to each treated data set, naming the fields dropped, the values coarsened or banded and the records held back, with a before-and-after extract from one of them.

title.en: Review the identification retained against current purposes

description.en: For each data action, confirm the identification it still carries is required by the purpose it serves today rather than by a purpose it once served. List the actions where identification could now be reduced and name the owner of each reduction.

evidenceHint.en: Review list showing each data action, the identification retained, the purpose relied on, and whether a reduction was raised.

templates.title: Limiting inferences about individuals
templates.description: Implements CT.DP-P3: Data are processed to limit the formulation of inferences about individuals' behavior or activities (e.g., data processing is decentralized, distributed architectures).
templates.objective: To ensure analytic outputs cannot be used to deduce an individual's behaviour or activity beyond the conclusions the organisation has agreed may be drawn from them.
templates.successCriteria:
A signed-off schedule names the conclusions barred outright and those permitted only above a stated group size.
Every analysis that releases output has a technique applied and an aggregation floor or band width in force, set by a named owner.
Each barred deduction has been attempted against the outputs the system actually releases, with the result recorded.
Where an attempt succeeded, the analysis design or its minimum group size was changed rather than the finding merely noted.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the signed-off schedule of off-limits conclusions, marking those barred outright and those limited by group size.
Collect the per-analysis configuration list naming the technique applied, the aggregation floor or band width, and the owner who set it.
Gather the dated inference-attempt reports covering the period.
Retrieve samples of the outputs the system released, including slices covering small populations.

Analysis:
Attempt one barred deduction against the released sample using only material a recipient would hold.
Check the aggregation floor enforced by the running analysis against the figure recorded in the configuration list.
Examine whether any released slice falls below the minimum group size stated for that conclusion.
Compare the inference-attempt reports with the changes made afterwards to see whether a successful attempt forced a redesign.

Output:
The assessor's inference-attempt record naming each conclusion tried, the material used and the result.
A configuration comparison of the floors recorded against the floors enforced in production.
A list of released outputs breaching a stated group size, with the analysis and its owner named.

title.en: List the deductions about behaviour and activity that must stay out of reach

description.en: A limit on inference is unenforceable until someone writes down which conclusions are off-limits: that a person was home on a Tuesday afternoon, that a household's occupancy changed, that somebody in a group is likely unwell. Work from the purpose each analysis actually serves, name the conclusions that reach past it, and separate those barred outright from those permitted only at group level above a stated size. Without that list every design argument collapses into whether the data is anonymous, which is a different question — an anonymous feed can still say what a household does each morning.

evidenceHint.en: Signed-off schedule of off-limits conclusions per analysis, marking which are barred outright and which are allowed only above a stated group size.

title.en: Reshape each analytic output so the barred conclusions cannot be drawn

description.en: De-identifying the inputs does not stop a result from announcing when a household wakes up, so the limit has to sit on what an analysis emits and not only on the records behind it. For each analysis pick whatever combination keeps a barred conclusion from following — computing where the data already sits and returning only totals, widening time and location bands, suppressing any cell below the agreed group size, or dropping a derived field nobody has a use for — and write the chosen setting beside the analysis it governs. Leave the reasoning attached, because a suppression threshold later relaxed for query performance will otherwise pass as routine tuning.

evidenceHint.en: Per-analysis configuration list naming the technique applied, the aggregation floor or band width in force, and the owner who set it.

title.en: Attempt each forbidden deduction against the outputs the system releases

description.en: Hand the released outputs to people who did not build the pipeline, together with whatever can be obtained publicly about the same population, and ask them to state what they can work out about one individual and about a small group. A deduction that fails only because this period's sample happened to be thin is not a control, so record against each attempt whether the design blocked it or the data did. Where an attempt succeeds, log the finding against the analysis that emitted the output rather than the store it drew from, because that is where the remedy has to go.

evidenceHint.en: Dated inference-attempt report listing each conclusion tried, the material used, the result, and whether design or sample size stopped it.

templates.title: Selective collection and disclosure settings
templates.description: Implements CT.DP-P4: System or device configurations permit selective collection or disclosure of data elements.
templates.objective: To ensure systems and devices can be set to gather and release only the data elements chosen, and that those settings still hold after a rebuild or an upgrade.
templates.successCriteria:
A written standard states which data elements every system must expose as individually controllable and which may be handled as a group.
Each system's collection and disclosure choices are recorded, and any product short of the standard was accepted by the named arbiter through the stated route.
Settings read back from a live machine after a rebuild, re-provision or version change match the values expected of it.
Choices newly offered by an upgraded system are either taken up or declined with a reason on the record.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the written selectivity standard with the individually controllable elements, the elements that may be grouped, and the acceptance route.
Collect the per-system record of the collection and disclosure choices each product offers.
Gather the period's list of rebuilds, re-provisions and version changes.
Retrieve the settings read back from those live machines with the expected values set beside them.

Analysis:
Read the live configuration of a sample of systems and compare each element against the value the record claims for it.
Check every acceptance granted to a product falling short of the standard for the arbiter's decision and the reasoning behind it.
Date each divergence found and determine whether it began at a rebuild, at an upgrade, or with a manual change.
Assess whether the choices introduced by a new version were evaluated and then adopted or declined on the record.

Output:
A standard-against-capability table for the systems sampled.
Drift findings naming each setting that differs from the expected value and the date it moved.
A list of accepted shortfalls with their arbiter and reasoning, and of newly available choices left unused.

title.en: Set the minimum selectivity a system must offer over what it gathers and sends

description.en: Before any product is examined, state the finest split the organisation expects to be able to make: which elements must be switchable on their own, which may be handled together as a group, and which are never optional. Without that standard the record of what each product allows has nothing to be judged against, and an all-or-nothing device passes simply because its single switch was written down. Name who may accept a product that cannot make the required split, and what they must put in writing when they do.

evidenceHint.en: Written standard listing the elements that must be individually controllable, those that may be grouped, the acceptance route for a product unable to meet it, and the named arbiter.

title.en: Record the collection and disclosure choices each system offers

description.en: For each system or device that allows a choice of which data elements are collected or released, record the setting in force, who set it and when it was last changed. Where a system offers no such choice, record that and name the owner who accepted collecting or releasing everything.

title.en: Re-check what each rebuilt or upgraded system now collects and releases

description.en: A selective setting is not done once: a re-image, a fleet re-provision or a vendor upgrade restores the supplier's default, and that default is almost always to gather and send everything on offer. For every system rebuilt, re-provisioned or upgraded since the last pass, read the setting back off the system itself rather than from the note made when it was first applied, and look for choices a newer release has added that nobody has taken up. Treat a reverted setting as a finding with a date attached, because how long it stood is the measure of what was gathered or released in the meantime.

evidenceHint.en: Per-system list of every rebuild, re-provision and version change in the period, the value read back from the live machine, the value expected, the date each divergence began, and any newly available choice left unused.

templates.title: Attribute references in place of values
templates.description: Implements CT.DP-P5: Attribute references are substituted for attribute values.
templates.objective: To ensure a reference stands in for an attribute value wherever one will serve, and that the reference itself discloses nothing the original value would have revealed.
templates.successCriteria:
Agreed criteria state how a reference may be derived, what residual meaning it may carry, and the form required in each case, each condition with an approver.
Every place where a reference stands in for an attribute value is recorded alongside the value it displaced.
Downstream copies, extracts, log sinks and reports have been swept, and any original attribute still found there is traced to what put it back.
References in use satisfy the derivation rule rather than being a readable encoding of the value they replace.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the agreed criteria for a valid substitution, with the reasoning and the approver recorded for each condition.
Collect the record of every attribute value currently replaced by a reference and the place the substitution happens.
Gather the dated sweep results listing the copies, extracts, log sinks and reports examined.
Retrieve a sample of stored references from a production data store.

Analysis:
Test whether a sampled reference can be turned back into its attribute value using the derivation rule and the material held beside it.
Search the downstream stores independently for the replaced attribute and compare what is found against the sweep results.
Determine for each surviving value whether an old load or a newer integration introduced it.
Check that the reference form in use for each case matches the form the criteria require.

Output:
An inventory of substitutions with the reference form and derivation in use for each.
Findings from the assessor's own downstream search, naming every store still holding the original value.
The reversal test result for the sampled references.

title.en: Fix the properties a reference must have before it replaces a value

description.en: Decide ahead of any build whether a reference may be computed from the value it displaces, how much residual meaning it may carry, and which form a given case calls for: an opaque token that resolves only through a held mapping, or a derived assertion such as a band or a yes-or-no claim that resolves back to nothing. A reference calculated from its own value, a hash of an email address or a shortened account number, is not a substitution at all, because anyone with a list of plausible values recomputes it and reads the field. Written as conditions a proposed design is tested against, these properties stop each team settling the question privately and give a later check something it can fail.

evidenceHint.en: Agreed criteria for a valid substitution covering permitted derivation, residual meaning and the form required per case, with the reasoning and the approver for each condition.

title.en: Record where a reference stands in place of an attribute value

description.en: List the places where a stand-in is held instead of the value it represents, what each stands for, where the mapping back to the value lives, and who is able to resolve it. Record the places where the value itself is still held although a stand-in would serve.

title.en: Sweep the downstream stores for values a reference was meant to replace

description.en: A substitution holds only at the point it was applied, and the displaced value returns downstream by routes nobody rebuilt: an extract taken before the change, a support tool that writes the field into its diagnostics, a warehouse column still loaded from an older feed, a row carrying the reference and the original side by side. Work outward through the copies rather than re-reading the system where the reference is issued, because that system is the one place the substitution is already known to hold. For each original value found, settle whether it predates the substitution or a newer path reintroduced it, since only the second means the design is being bypassed and the store will fill again after a clean-up.

evidenceHint.en: Dated results listing every copy, extract, log sink and report examined, each original attribute still found in one, and whether an old load or a new integration put it there.

templates.title: Transparency policies and procedures
templates.description: Implements CM.PO-P1: Transparency policies, processes, and procedures for communicating data processing purposes, practices, associated privacy risks, and options for enabling individuals' data processing preferences and requests are established and in place.
templates.objective: To ensure the organisation has settled what it will tell individuals about its processing, and that approving a change to that processing sets the telling in motion.
templates.successCriteria:
A transparency policy states the purposes, practices, privacy risks and preference options that must be conveyed to individuals.
The issued procedure names the approval that opens the transparency step and the period allowed before individuals hear of the change.
A recent processing change can be followed from its approval through to the communication it produced, inside that period.
Sampled communications carry the content the policy requires, and every omission found has an identified cause.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the transparency policy setting out what individuals are told about processing purposes, practices and privacy risks.
Collect the issued procedure showing the triggering approval and the time allowed before individuals are informed.
Gather the approval records for processing changes made during the period.
Retrieve the communications issued in the same period together with the sample check performed against the policy.

Analysis:
Select approved processing changes and trace each to the communication it produced, measuring the elapsed time against the period allowed.
Compare a sample of issued communications with the policy's content requirements point by point.
Identify approved changes that produced no communication at all and establish why the trigger did not fire.
Assess whether the options for exercising preferences and requests are described wherever the policy requires them.

Output:
A trace table of processing changes against the communications and dates they produced.
A point-by-point content comparison of the sampled communications against the policy.
A list of approved changes with no communication issued, and of omissions with their causes.

title.en: Define what the organisation will tell individuals about its data processing

description.en: State which purposes, practices, privacy risks and available options must be communicated, and on what occasions a communication becomes owed — at collection, at a change, on request, after an event. Attach the transparency policy; it is the standard a later sample check measures issued communications against.

title.en: Trigger the transparency step from the approval of a processing change

description.en: Tie the transparency step to the approval that lets processing change — a new purpose, a new recipient, a shortened retention — so it opens before the change reaches individuals rather than when somebody remembers the policy exists. Fix how long a communication may lag the change it describes, name who hears about it when that period is running out, and have the functions granting those approvals acknowledge the step binds them. A procedure driven instead from the communications side always describes last quarter's processing, and the gap surfaces only when an individual compares what they were told against what is actually done.

evidenceHint.en: The issued procedure naming which approval opens the step, the period allowed before individuals hear of the change, and one recent change walked through it.

title.en: Check a sample of issued communications against the transparency policy

description.en: Take communications actually issued since the last check and confirm each covered what the policy requires for its occasion. Record every omission, the role that approved the communication, and whether the gap lies in the communication or in the policy.

evidenceHint.en: Sample check naming the communications reviewed, the policy points each was measured against, and every omission found with its cause.

templates.title: Roles for communicating data processing
templates.description: Implements CM.PO-P2: Roles and responsibilities (e.g., public relations) for communicating data processing purposes, practices, and associated privacy risks are established.
templates.objective: To ensure a named person is answerable for drafting, approving and speaking each privacy communication, and that cover exists whenever the holder is unavailable.
templates.successCriteria:
Each of the drafting, approving and issuing roles for privacy communications has a named holder and a named stand-in.
The standing list of holders is published where staff can reach it and was refreshed in the period, with every reassignment dated.
Every privacy communication issued in the period resolves to a drafter, an approver and a speaker.
Items issued without approval or by someone outside the assigned role carry a recorded decision.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the role definitions for drafting, approving and issuing communications about data processing.
Collect the standing list of holders and stand-ins, together with the location where it is published.
Gather the dated reassignments made since the previous refresh of that list.
Retrieve the attribution table covering the period's communications, and the communications themselves.

Analysis:
Confirm each named holder and stand-in is in post by comparing the standing list against current staffing records.
Trace a sample of issued communications through the attribution table to the approval record behind each one.
Check whether any communication was issued by a person outside the assigned role, or with no approver named at all.
Assess whether the published list was genuinely reachable by the staff expected to consult it.

Output:
A role-to-holder schedule with stand-ins and the date each was last confirmed.
Attribution findings for the sampled communications, naming any with a missing or unauthorised approver.
A record of the decisions taken on unapproved or misrouted items.

title.en: Assign the roles that draft, approve and issue privacy communications

description.en: Name the role that drafts a privacy communication, the role that approves its content, and the role that speaks when a privacy matter reaches the public, and record where the boundary between them sits and who acts when one is unavailable. Record the assignment against the named roles rather than against individuals who may move.

title.en: Refresh the holder and stand-in for every communication role each period

description.en: An assignment names roles, but a role with no occupant behind it cannot approve or speak, so each period carry every named communication role through to a person today and an identified cover, and record the reassignments made since the last pass. Publish it where anyone fielding a question about the organisation's data processing can see who holds the role now, instead of routing it to whoever answered last time. Keep the dated history alongside the current state: a communication issued three months ago has to be attributable to whoever held the approval then, not to whoever holds it today.

evidenceHint.en: The standing list of who holds each communication role and who covers for them, showing where it is published and the dated reassignments made since the previous update.

title.en: Trace each privacy communication back to the person who approved it

description.en: Take the privacy communications and public statements made since the last review and name, for each, who drafted it, who signed it off and who delivered it, then set that against the roles the assignment gives those jobs to; whether the content itself was adequate is a separate check. The failures worth finding are the item that went out with no sign-off at all, and the one approved by whichever senior person happened to be reachable — both mean the organisation is running on something other than the assignment it wrote down. Where a named holder repeatedly did not perform their part, decide whether the assignment moves or the behaviour does, and record which was chosen.

evidenceHint.en: Attribution table covering the period's communications with drafter, approver and speaker set against the assigned roles, listing every unapproved or misrouted item and the decision taken on it.

templates.title: Mechanisms for communicating data processing
templates.description: Implements CM.AW-P1: Mechanisms (e.g., notices, internal or public reports) for communicating data processing purposes, practices, associated privacy risks, and options for enabling individuals' preferences and requests are established and in place.
templates.objective: To ensure everything the organisation must tell individuals has a working channel, an artefact that carries it, and a despatch record showing that it went out.
templates.successCriteria:
Every required communication is mapped to the channel that delivers it to the individuals concerned.
The notice and the periodic report exist as issued artefacts, each bearing a version marker, an issue date and the channel it was placed in.
Periodic reports were despatched during the period, with their recipients and dates recorded.
Each superseded notice version names the processing change that forced its replacement.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the scoping list mapping each required communication to the channel that carries it to individuals.
Collect the notice as an individual sees it and the report as circulated, with version markers and issue dates.
Gather the issue log for the period showing reports despatched, their recipients and dates.
Retrieve the superseded notice versions and the processing changes recorded against them.

Analysis:
Open each named channel as an individual would and confirm the notice live there is the version held on file.
Check the despatch dates of the periodic reports against the frequency the scoping list commits to.
Match each notice reissue to the processing change recorded as its cause, and look for changes that produced no reissue.
Verify the report covers the processing practices and privacy risks the scoping list assigns to that artefact.

Output:
A channel-by-channel confirmation of the notice version live at the time of test.
A despatch record for the period's reports with their recipients and dates.
A version history of the notice with the processing change behind each replacement.

title.en: Record how each required communication reaches individuals

description.en: For every item the transparency policy requires be communicated, record the means by which it currently reaches individuals or the public, where it sits today, and when it was last changed. Where an item is required but reaches nobody, record that as an open row with an owner.

title.en: Build the notice and the report that each named channel will carry

description.en: Turn each entry on the channel list into an artefact that actually exists: the notice a person meets at the point of collection, the internal report that reaches management, the public report if one has been promised. Each has to carry the purposes, the practices and the privacy risks in language its audience can act on, and — the part most often left out — what the individual may ask for and where to ask for it. A notice that explains the processing but names no route for a preference or a request is only half a mechanism, and the symptom is requests arriving at whatever address people can find. Where the channel list showed a communication that is owed but has no artefact behind it, this is where that gap closes.

evidenceHint.en: The artefacts as issued — the notice as an individual sees it and the report as it was circulated — each carrying a version marker, an issue date, and the channel from the scoping list it was placed in.

title.en: Send out each periodic report and reissue the notice when processing changes

description.en: A mechanism counts as in place only while it is being worked: the periodic report has to go out on the cadence it claims, and the notice has to be replaced once the processing it describes has moved on. The failure here is quiet — a new purpose, a new recipient or a longer retention goes live while the published notice still describes last year's arrangement, leaving the organisation on record saying something that is no longer true. Treat any change that would alter a sentence of the notice as the trigger to reissue, rather than waiting for an annual refresh. Keep the superseded version instead of overwriting it, because a later question about what someone was told will be about the wording live on the day they were told it.

evidenceHint.en: Issue log for the period: each report despatched with its date and who received it, each notice version superseded, and the processing change that forced the replacement.

templates.title: Mechanisms for obtaining individual feedback
templates.description: Implements CM.AW-P2: Mechanisms for obtaining feedback from individuals (e.g., surveys or focus groups) about data processing and associated privacy risks are established and in place.
templates.objective: To ensure the organisation actively asks the people whose data it processes what they make of that processing, and finds out which of them never answer.
templates.successCriteria:
Every category of individuals whose data is processed has a feedback instrument aimed at it and an owner who collects what it receives.
Solicitations made during the period record who was asked, when they were asked, and what came back.
Responses are counted by category, so a category that returned nothing is visible rather than absorbed into a total.
Each silent category carries a stated reason and an agreed change to the instrument that failed to reach it.
Changes considered or made are recorded against the feedback that prompted them.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the feedback instruments as they currently stand, including question wording, session plans and forms.
Collect the mapping of each instrument to the category of individuals it is meant to reach and to its owner.
Gather the solicitation records for the period showing who was asked and what came back.
Retrieve the reach and response counts per category with the reasons recorded for silent categories.

Analysis:
Compare the categories of individuals appearing in the processing inventory with the categories an instrument actually reaches.
Read the question wording and session plans for items that would deter or bias a response on privacy matters.
Examine the categories reporting no responses and test the stated reason against the way that instrument was distributed.
Trace feedback received through to the changes considered or made, and note feedback that reached no decision.

Output:
A coverage map of individual categories against feedback instruments and their owners.
A response analysis by category naming the silent ones and the instrument changes agreed against them.
A list of feedback items with the change or decision recorded for each.

title.en: Fit feedback instruments to the populations whose data is processed

description.en: Take the categories of individuals the processing touches and decide, for each, the means by which the organisation will ask them what they make of it — a questionnaire, a moderated session, a standing panel, an open form — then stand that means up so it is capable of receiving an answer today rather than in principle. One instrument rarely covers everyone: people who never sign in cannot see an in-product prompt, former customers no longer receive the mailing, and a group whose data arrived through an employer, a school or a broker has no direct line at all. Give each instrument a named owner and a destination the responses actually land in, because a route nobody empties has not been established, only announced.

evidenceHint.en: The instruments as they currently stand — question wording, session plan, form — listed against the category of individuals each is meant to reach and the owner who empties it.

title.en: Solicit individuals' views on the processing and record what came back

description.en: Ask individuals directly what they make of the processing and the risks it carries, by whatever means suits the population, and record the responses received and what was done with them. This is the organisation going to individuals; complaints arriving unprompted are handled through the monitoring intake instead.

evidenceHint.en: Record of the solicitation showing who was asked, when, what came back, and the changes considered or made as a result.

title.en: Judge each feedback route by who actually answered it

description.en: Set the responses arriving since the last check against the categories of individuals the processing covers, and note for each route how many people it was capable of reaching as well as how many replied. A route that returns nothing is ambiguous — it can mean contentment, or that it reached no one — so state which of the two the evidence supports instead of letting an empty inbox pass as approval. Where a category has stayed silent across two checks running, name the instrument that will be changed for it and the person changing it.

evidenceHint.en: Reach and response counts per category of individuals for the period, with a stated reason for every silent category and the instrument change agreed against it.

templates.title: In-product data processing visibility
templates.description: Implements CM.AW-P3: System/product/service design enables data processing visibility.
templates.objective: To ensure a person using the product can see from the product itself what it does with data about them, for which purpose, and to whom that data goes.
templates.successCriteria:
Each system has a record of what its interface shows an individual about the processing of their own data.
A dated walkthrough driven from a test account exists, setting the screens an individual sees against the processing that actually ran.
Every element, purpose or recipient the processing touched but the interface never named is listed as a blind spot.
Data actions added or altered in the period were reviewed for visibility, and each accepted blind spot has an owner and a reasoning.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the per-system record of what the interface discloses to an individual about their own data.
Collect the dated walkthrough notes naming the test account used and the screens visited.
Gather processing logs or data-flow records covering that same account over the walkthrough period.
Retrieve the design review minutes covering data actions added or altered during the period.

Analysis:
Drive the product from a test account and set what the interface names against what the logs show was actually processed.
Identify the elements, purposes and recipients present in the processing but absent from every screen an individual can reach.
Compare each newly added data action with the interface change, if any, made to expose it.
Assess whether accepted blind spots carry an owner and a reasoning rather than being left undecided.

Output:
A walkthrough record from the assessor's own session, screen by screen.
A gap list of the elements, purposes and recipients the product never surfaces.
A schedule of data actions reviewed for visibility with the owner of each accepted blind spot.

title.en: Record what each system shows an individual about the processing of their data

description.en: For every system with which individuals interact directly, record what they can see about what is being done with their data and what options they can exercise there. Where a system shows nothing, record that and name the owner of the decision to leave it so.

title.en: Drive the product as an individual and compare its view to what ran

description.en: An in-product view built from a hand-written summary drifts the moment a feature starts reading a new element, and nobody notices because the screen still renders. Sign in to a genuine account that has real activity behind it, visit every place the product claims to tell the person what is happening to their data, and set the elements, purposes and recipients named on screen against those the system actually touched for that account. Anything the processing did that no screen accounts for is the finding, not the pass.

evidenceHint.en: Dated walkthrough per system naming the test account, the screens visited, and every element, purpose or recipient the processing touched that the interface never named.

title.en: Challenge designs that leave a data action invisible inside the product

description.en: Visibility is decided at design time, so the gap appears in a specification rather than in a test run: a feature is built with no screen, indicator or setting through which the person would ever learn it ran. Take the data actions added or altered since the last cycle and, for each one with nowhere in the interface an individual could see it, force a ruling — the design gains a surface, or a named owner accepts the blind spot and states why. A published notice is not an answer here, because what is under examination is what the product itself reveals to the person using it.

evidenceHint.en: Design review minutes listing each data action added or altered in the period, whether the interface exposes it, and the owner and reasoning behind every accepted blind spot.

templates.title: Records of data disclosures and sharing
templates.description: Implements CM.AW-P4: Records of data disclosures and sharing are maintained and can be accessed for review or transmission/disclosure.
templates.objective: To ensure that every disclosure or onward sharing of personal data leaves a retrievable record, so an account of who received an individual's data can be produced on demand.
templates.successCriteria:
Every outbound sharing path is bound to a ledger entry marked system-written or person-written.
Ledger entries carry the recipient, the data shared, the date and the provenance of the values sent, with no required field blank.
A disclosure account for one named individual can be extracted without reconstructing it from the sending systems.
Reconciliation against independent sending sources finds no transfer that reached a recipient without a usable entry.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the register of outbound sharing paths with the system-written or person-written marking against each.
Collect one populated ledger entry per path type, showing every required field as captured in production.
Request a disclosure account extracted for one named individual, with the date it was produced.
Gather the latest reconciliation worksheet and the independent sources it names.

Analysis:
Compare the path register against the systems and contracts that actually move data outward to find unledgered routes.
Test sampled entries for blank or defaulted fields, concentrating on person-written paths where capture depends on an operator.
Re-run the individual extract against the raw ledger to confirm it returns every held disclosure and none belonging to another subject.
Trace each reconciliation gap to the path that produced it and confirm an owner and a remediation date were recorded.

Output:
An annotated path register marking each route ledgered, partial or uncovered.
A field-completeness finding for the sampled entries, broken out by path type.
A verdict on whether an individual's disclosure account can be produced on request.
A list of unledgered transfers carried forward to remediation.

title.en: Attach a ledger entry to each outbound sharing path

description.en: Walk the paths by which data actually leaves — scheduled feeds to processors, partner APIs, bulk exports, files a support or sales person sends, answers given to a law-enforcement or regulator request — and bind each one to an entry carrying the recipient, the date, the data elements, the individuals covered and the authorisation relied on. Say for every path whether the entry is written by the system performing the transfer or by a person, because the paths with no system behind them are exactly where the ledger quietly stops being complete. Index entries by individual and by recipient at the point they are written; a ledger that can only be read chronologically cannot answer 'who received this person's data' without a full scan.

evidenceHint.en: The path list with each outbound path marked system-written or person-written, plus one populated entry per path type showing every required field filled.

title.en: Record disclosures, sharing and provenance so an individual account can be produced

description.en: Capture, for each disclosure or sharing of data, what was disclosed, to whom and when, and capture for received data where it came from and through whom, in a form that can be retrieved and released on request. Test the retrieval by producing one account end to end.

evidenceHint.en: An extract produced from the disclosure and provenance records for one named individual or data set, with the date it was produced.

title.en: Find the disclosures that happened but never reached the ledger

description.en: Start from evidence that data went out which the ledger did not produce — processor and partner contracts, egress and API logs, the legal-request file, invoices from data recipients — and look for a matching entry for each transfer those sources show. This failure is silent in the other direction: a ledger holding nothing reads exactly like a quarter in which nothing was shared, so only an outside source can tell the two apart. Count entries that exist but cannot be used as misses too — a recipient recorded as a team name, a missing date, a referenced export that has since been deleted — and check the surviving entries still cover the period a review or an individual's request may reach back into.

evidenceHint.en: Reconciliation worksheet naming each independent source consulted, the transfers it showed, which had a usable entry, and every gap with the path that produced it.

templates.title: Communicating corrections and deletions
templates.description: Implements CM.AW-P5: Data corrections or deletions can be communicated to individuals or organizations (e.g., data sources) in the data processing ecosystem.
templates.objective: To ensure a correction or erasure made to personal data travels onward to every party that previously received it, and that the individual is told the change took effect.
templates.successCriteria:
A routing list names, for each prior recipient, the contact, the message form, the sending window and whether onward relay is required.
Corrections and deletions reach downstream recipients inside the agreed window, not at the next convenient batch.
Individuals receive the standing confirmation wording telling them the change was applied and passed on.
Recipients that could not be reached are recorded with the cause and stay open until resolved.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the recipient routing list with contact, message form, sending window and relay obligation for each party.
Collect the standing confirmation wording issued to individuals after a correction or erasure.
Gather the period's notification records naming the change made, the parties told and the date of each dispatch.
Request the two outward trace walkthroughs, including the confirmations returned by recipients.

Analysis:
Match the routing list against sharing agreements and transfer records to find recipients with no notification route defined.
Time each notification from the date the change was applied to the date it was sent, against the agreed window.
Check every party marked unreachable for a follow-up attempt and a decision rather than silent closure.
Re-walk one traced case independently to confirm the cited acknowledgements exist and cover the same data.

Output:
A coverage finding on prior recipients lacking a defined notification route.
Dispatch timeliness measured separately for corrections and for deletions in the period.
A register of parties left untold, with the cause recorded against each.
An assessment of whether individuals were confirmed to in the agreed wording.

title.en: Establish the route by which a correction or erasure reaches each prior recipient

description.en: For every organisation that has received personal data — processor, partner, onward recipient, or the source it came from — settle who receives the notice, in what form, within what window, and whether they must confirm back or pass it further down their own chain. Contracts routinely promise deletion on instruction while naming nobody to instruct, so the route does not exist until a live contact and an agreed message shape sit on both sides of it. Build the return leg at the same time: the individual who asked for the change needs to be told it was made and how far it travelled, rather than left to infer it from a screen that now looks different.

evidenceHint.en: The routing list — each recipient organisation with its named contact, the agreed message form, the sending window, and whether onward relay is required — alongside the standing wording used to confirm a change back to the individual.

title.en: Notify the ecosystem parties holding data when it is corrected or deleted

description.en: When a correction or deletion is made, tell the parties that previously received the data or supplied it, and record who was told, what they were told and when. Record the parties that could not be told and what stands in the way.

evidenceHint.en: Notification record naming the change made, the parties told, the date, and any party that could not be reached.

title.en: Trace a completed correction and deletion outward to the parties that received the data

description.en: Take one correction and one deletion that were actually carried out, and follow each outward: who was sent notice, who confirmed they applied it, and what the individual was told. The gap that keeps appearing is a party that received the data before the route was set up; the second is a party that acknowledged the notice without acting on it, since an acknowledgement proves receipt and never that the record changed at their end. Where someone was missed, separate a miss caused by an incomplete recipient list from one caused by a notice that was never sent, because those two failures are fixed in different places.

evidenceHint.en: The two walked-through cases, each showing the change made, who was contacted, the confirmations returned, what the individual received, and any party found untold with the reason it happened.

templates.title: Data provenance and lineage
templates.description: Implements CM.AW-P6: Data provenance and lineage are maintained and can be accessed for review or transmission/disclosure.
templates.objective: To ensure the origin and derivation of personal data elements remain reconstructible, so the organisation can say where a value came from and what it was computed from.
templates.successCriteria:
An element-level origin register gives each attribute its source type, named supplier or computation inputs, first holding system and entry date.
New feeds, copies and derived sets enter the lineage record as they are built, naming the transformation and who entered it.
A reviewer unaided by the builders can trace a derived attribute back to its collected sources within the stated time.
Hops that cannot be established are named as gaps with an assigned owner rather than left blank.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the element-level origin register covering the attributes held about individuals.
Collect the dated lineage additions and amendments made during the period.
Request the independent trace walkthrough, the attribute it examined and the elapsed time recorded.
Gather the inventory of feeds, extracts and derived data sets built in the same period.

Analysis:
Reconcile the period's new feeds and derived sets against the lineage additions to find builds that never registered.
Inspect register rows for placeholder sources such as "internal" or "legacy" that name no supplier or computation.
Select a derived attribute yourself and attempt the trace unaided, comparing effort and result with the recorded walkthrough.
Confirm every unestablished hop carries an owner and a date by which the ancestry will be settled.

Output:
Lineage coverage expressed by attribute and by system of first capture.
A list of data sets built in the period with no corresponding lineage record.
The assessor's own trace result beside the organisation's, with any divergence noted.
An inventory of unresolved ancestry gaps and the owners assigned to them.

title.en: Capture where each data element originated and what it was derived from

description.en: Against every element already inventoried, note how the organisation came to hold it: supplied by the individual, observed by a device or service, bought or received from a named party, or computed from other elements. Elements the organisation works out for itself need the inputs that fed them named, or a later question about an attribute the individual never gave has no answer. A value copied between stores keeps the origin of the place it was first collected — recording the nearest upstream table instead is the common way provenance quietly becomes useless.

evidenceHint.en: Element-level origin register listing source type, the named supplier or the computation inputs, the first system to hold the value, and the date it entered.

title.en: Extend the lineage whenever a new feed, copy or derived set is built

description.en: Every new extract, vendor feed, replica or derived table has its inputs and transformation added to the lineage before anything consumes it, and a rewired pipeline has its existing entry corrected rather than left standing. Lineage decays silently: nothing fails when a job changes its source, so the recorded path stays plausible while being wrong. The usual offender is a set built for a one-off analysis that becomes a standing input to something else without ever being registered.

evidenceHint.en: Dated lineage additions and amendments for the period, each naming the flow, its inputs, the transformation applied, and who entered it.

title.en: Reconstruct a derived attribute's ancestry without help from its builders

description.en: Choose a value the organisation produced rather than collected and have someone outside the team that built it trace it back through every hop to the point of collection, using only the maintained lineage. Note how long the trace took and where it needed a person who simply remembered; ancestry only its authors can rebuild is not accessible in the sense this outcome requires. Name every hop that could not be established and the owner who will restore it.

evidenceHint.en: Trace walkthrough naming the value chosen, the reviewer, each hop confirmed or unestablished, the elapsed time, and the owners assigned to the gaps.

templates.title: Notifying those impacted by a privacy event
templates.description: Implements CM.AW-P7: Impacted individuals and organizations are notified about a privacy breach or event.
templates.objective: To ensure individuals and organisations affected by a privacy breach are told what happened and what is open to them, quickly enough to act and without anyone being missed.
templates.successCriteria:
Standing notice content states what occurred, the data involved, the steps taken and what the recipient may do, written before any event.
Each dispatch record fixes the impacted-list cut-off, the counts sent per audience and route, and the notice version issued.
Every entry in the impacted set carries a delivery outcome, with bounces escalated to substitute notice rather than closed unsent.
Discovery-to-delivery is measured per party and sits within the notification deadline the organisation is held to.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the standing notification content and the audiences it is written for.
Collect the dispatch record for each privacy event in the period, including the list cut-off timestamp.
Gather the bounce and substitute-notice tally for those same events.
Request the closed event's impacted set with a delivery outcome recorded beside every entry.

Analysis:
Read the standing content against the notification duties the organisation is subject to and note any required element absent.
Recount recipients by audience and route, comparing the totals with the impacted set as it stood at cut-off.
Calculate discovery-to-delivery for a sample of parties and test each against the deadline claimed.
Follow every bounced entry to a substitute notice, a later successful send, or an open item with a named owner.

Output:
A gap analysis of the standing notice content against the elements required of it.
Recipient counts recomputed by the assessor beside the counts the organisation reported.
A distribution of notification intervals, naming any party notified past the deadline.
A list of impacted parties with no confirmed delivery and the owner of each.

title.en: Record what impacted individuals are told and offered after a privacy event

description.en: State what a notification to an affected individual must contain, who issues it, and which mitigation options the organisation is prepared to offer — a correction, a deletion, a withdrawal of an authorisation, or another remedy. Attach the notification content and the list of remedies so neither has to be invented under pressure.

title.en: Dispatch the breach notice to each impacted individual and affected organisation

description.en: Once an event is confirmed, put the notice out on the routes actually held for both audiences — the individuals whose data was involved, and the organisations caught in the same event, including any that received the affected data from us. The impacted list is usually still growing while the first wave goes out, so state the cut-off the list was drawn at and treat anyone added afterwards as a second wave rather than quietly extending the first. Contact details held for a closed account are routinely stale, so capture the bounces and say which substitute route carried the notice to the people direct contact could not reach.

evidenceHint.en: Per-event dispatch record: the list cut-off timestamp, recipient counts broken out by audience and route, which version of the notice went, and the bounce and substitute-notice tally.

title.en: Prove that every party found impacted received a notification

description.en: After the event is closed, take the impacted set the investigation finally settled on and check each entry in it against a delivery outcome — not the send list against itself, which will confirm itself and silently omit everyone added when the scope widened. Measure when notification landed against the deadline that applied, counted from discovery rather than from when the notice was drafted. Flag any organisation reached only through a commercial or account contact instead of a named privacy contact; that is the case most likely to have gone nowhere.

evidenceHint.en: The closed event's impacted set with a delivery outcome beside every entry, the discovery-to-delivery interval per party, and any entry still unresolved carried forward with a named owner.

templates.title: Mitigation offered after a privacy event
templates.description: Implements CM.AW-P8: Individuals are provided with mitigation mechanisms (e.g., credit monitoring, consent withdrawal, data alteration or deletion) to address impacts of problematic data actions.
templates.objective: To ensure individuals harmed by a problematic data action can actually obtain a remedy, with the means to deliver it arranged in advance rather than improvised after the event.
templates.successCriteria:
Each remedy on offer rests on a signed supplier agreement or a funding approval dated before the event it would answer.
An individual can activate every offered remedy by following a documented path, without contacting the organisation to learn how.
Every offer made is followed to take-up, refusal or lapse, with the reason recorded where it lapsed unused.
Harm types seen in the period are matched to available remedies, and each unmatched harm carries a named owner and a decision.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the supplier agreements and funding approvals underpinning each remedy, with their effective dates.
Collect the documented activation path an individual follows for each remedy offered.
Request the per-individual tracking extract showing the outcome reached against every offer in the period.
Gather the harm-to-remedy comparison and the uptake figures recorded in it.

Analysis:
Check each agreement's effective date against the events it was relied on for, to identify remedies arranged retrospectively.
Attempt the activation path as an individual would, noting steps needing knowledge the notice does not supply.
Separate lapsed offers from refused ones in the tracking data and test whether lapses cluster on one remedy or one channel.
Compare the harms recorded in the period against the remedies available and confirm each unmatched harm reached a decision.

Output:
A schedule of remedies showing the date delivery capacity was secured for each.
A walkthrough finding on the activation path for every remedy type.
Take-up, refusal and lapse rates per remedy, with the causes of lapse summarised.
A list of harms for which no remedy was offered, with owners and decisions.

title.en: Stand up the enrolment route for every remedy on offer

description.en: A remedy named in an incident plan is worthless if nothing behind it can be activated on the day: a monitoring subscription with no contract means haggling over price while the take-up window closes, and a refund with no approved funding source stalls at the first approval. For each remedy the organisation is willing to put in front of an individual, settle the supplier agreement or internal funding decision in advance, and establish how an individual reaches it — the code, the claim form, the case line, the switch that actually withdraws an authorisation or erases a record. Give each one an eligibility test and a take-up deadline now, because both will otherwise be improvised by whoever answers the phone.

evidenceHint.en: Signed supplier agreements or funding approvals per remedy, together with the activation path an individual would follow, dated ahead of any event.

title.en: Follow each offered remedy through to take-up or refusal

description.en: Counting a remedy as delivered the moment the offer leaves the building hides the individual who never redeemed the code, whose refund was returned, or whose restoration case was opened and never worked. Carry a per-individual state from offer made to remedy in hand, and close each one with an outcome — used, declined, expired, or blocked with the obstacle named. Expiry is the common silent failure: offers lapse quietly and the organisation reads the resulting inaction as satisfaction.

evidenceHint.en: Per-individual tracking extract for the period showing the outcome reached against every offer, including those that lapsed unused and why.

title.en: Weigh each remedy against the harm it was meant to undo

description.en: Credit monitoring is the reflex offer and it addresses only a narrow band of harm — it does nothing about a health detail already published, a wrongful denial of service, or money already taken. Set the remedies actually available beside the problematic data actions the risk assessment identifies, and name every harm with no usable remedy behind it. Low take-up and complaints raised after a remedy was accepted are the signal that what was offered did not fit; judge adequacy on those, not on how many offers went out.

evidenceHint.en: The period's comparison of harm types against available remedies and their observed uptake, with each unmatched gap carrying a named owner and a decision.

templates.title: Baseline configuration for each class of system
templates.description: Implements PR.PO-P1: A baseline configuration of information technology is created and maintained incorporating security principles (e.g., concept of least functionality).
templates.objective: To ensure each class of system is built to a recorded configuration that leaves off what is not needed, so a new machine starts hardened instead of being remediated afterwards.
templates.successCriteria:
Every class of system in the estate has a recorded baseline stating the settings it must hold and the functionality it must not carry.
New systems are provisioned from a stored image, template or manifest that applies the baseline, not from manual build steps.
Each baseline value carries its origin in source guidance and a role accountable for keeping it current.
Baselines are re-derived when the platform release or guidance edition behind them moves, and classes holding none are identified.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the baseline configuration documents and the list of system classes they are written for.
Collect the provisioning artefact stored for each class - image, template or manifest - and the values it sets.
Gather the latest currency pass, naming the guidance release and edition each class was measured against.
Request an inventory of systems built during the period with the class assigned to each.

Analysis:
Compare the class list against the asset inventory to find running systems belonging to no documented class.
Read the provisioning artefacts against their baselines to identify settings documented but never applied at build time.
Check each recorded value for a stated origin and an accountable role, flagging those carried with neither.
Test the currency pass against the platform versions actually running, to find baselines measured on superseded guidance.

Output:
A coverage table of system classes against baselines and provisioning artefacts.
A list of baseline settings absent from the build artefact that claims to apply them.
A currency verdict per class, naming those measured against outdated guidance.
An inventory of system classes operating with no baseline at all.

title.en: Record the baseline configuration each class of system must meet

description.en: For each class of system, state the configuration it must start from, which capabilities are on and which are off before it enters service, and the conditions required of the space it physically operates in. Attach the baseline per class and name the role that owns it.

title.en: Turn each baseline into the build new systems are provisioned from

description.en: A baseline written as prose is read once and then ignored: the next machine is cloned from the one already running, and the standard quietly becomes a description of whatever got built rather than a rule the build has to satisfy. Express each class's baseline in the terms its platform actually uses — setting names and their values, the packages and services the build includes, the accounts that exist at first boot, the interfaces it opens — and hold it as the artefact provisioning begins from, so a system of that class cannot be stood up except through it. Note against each entry where it came from: a vendor default deliberately overridden, guidance the organisation chose to follow, or an internal decision taken for this class, because a later reader otherwise cannot tell a considered choice from an accident nobody dares touch.

evidenceHint.en: The stored provisioning artefact for every system class — image, template or manifest — showing the values it sets, the origin noted against each, and the role accountable for it.

title.en: Re-derive the baselines whose platform version or source guidance has since moved

description.en: A baseline rots against the world rather than against the estate: the vendor ships a release that renames or withdraws settings the baseline names, the guidance it was derived from is revised, or a class of system enters service with nothing written for it at all. Work forwards from the release notes and the guidance publishers instead of re-reading the baseline to judge whether it still looks sensible, because a document can be perfectly coherent and still describe a version nobody runs. Close the pass by stating, per class, whether its baseline was reaffirmed, amended or found to have no applicable version left, and by naming any class operating without one.

evidenceHint.en: Dated currency pass listing every system class, the release and edition of guidance it was measured against, the outcome reached, and each class found to have none.

templates.title: Configuration change control
templates.description: Implements PR.PO-P2: Configuration change control processes are established and in place.
templates.objective: To ensure configuration alterations are authorised at a level matching their consequence before reaching production, and that what was applied can be matched to what was approved.
templates.successCriteria:
A signed-off classification states, per change type, whether prior approval is required, the approving role and the urgent-route threshold.
Proposals, approvals and applied changes are recorded so an alteration found on a system can be matched back to its authorisation.
Urgent-route changes are ratified afterwards within the stated period rather than left unreviewed.
Reconciliation rebuilt from the systems leaves no production alteration without an approval or a recorded disposition.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the signed-off change classification with approving roles and urgent-route thresholds.
Collect the procedure describing how a change is proposed, approved and recorded.
Gather the period's approval records together with the change log the process maintains.
Request the reconciliation naming each system-side source of applied changes that was read.

Analysis:
Pull applied configuration changes directly from the systems and match each to an approval, rather than working from the approval list outward.
Test a sample of approvals for an approver holding the role the classification requires for that change type.
Examine urgent-route changes for after-the-fact ratification inside the stated period.
Review each unapproved alteration for a recorded disposition and an owner rather than closure without comment.

Output:
A match rate of applied changes to approvals, computed from the system side.
A list of approvals granted by someone other than the role the classification names.
An urgent-route summary showing ratification status for each change taken that way.
A schedule of unapproved alterations with the disposition agreed for each.

title.en: Decide which configuration alterations need approval before they reach a live system

description.en: Name the classes of change that must be proposed and approved first — a firewall rule, a retention setting, a schema migration, an access flag on a store holding personal data — and the everyday actions that may proceed without one, so nobody has to judge it at the keyboard. Where that boundary falls is what the whole process lives or dies on: set too wide it buries routine work in paperwork and people quietly stop filing, set too narrow it leaves the settings deciding who can read personal data outside any approval at all. State the depth of scrutiny each class earns and the point at which the urgent route may be used, because the change made at three in the morning is the one argued about afterwards.

evidenceHint.en: Signed-off classification of change types showing, for each, whether prior approval is required, the scrutiny it attracts, the approving role, and the threshold for the urgent route.

title.en: Define how a configuration change is proposed, approved and recorded

description.en: State who may propose a change to a system's configuration, what must be assessed before it is approved, who approves it, and what is written down when it is applied. Include how an urgent change is handled and what is done afterwards to bring it back into the record.

title.en: Rebuild the period's change list from the systems and find the changes no approval covers

description.en: Take what was actually altered from sources nobody edits to flatter themselves — deployment history, configuration management state, package and image versions, provider audit logs — and match each entry against the approvals on file, instead of reading the change log and judging whether it looks complete. Change control fails silently in one direction only: a change that was never proposed leaves nothing behind in the record to look missing. Account for every unmatched alteration, the urgent ones applied first and never written up included, and name who owns closing each gap.

evidenceHint.en: Dated reconciliation naming each source of applied changes read, every alteration found with no approval behind it, and the disposition agreed for each.

templates.title: Backups and proven restoration
templates.description: Implements PR.PO-P3: Backups of information are conducted, maintained, and tested.
templates.objective: To ensure personal data can be brought back after loss or corruption within the tolerance agreed for it, proven by restoring the data rather than by the backup job reporting success.
templates.successCriteria:
Every store holding personal data carries a tolerable loss window and a retention period on the coverage schedule, or a signed reason for omission.
Backup copies sit where production credentials cannot alter or delete them, with location, permitted credentials and encryption catalogued.
Failed, skipped or truncated runs are raised and followed up rather than absorbed by the next successful run.
A restore is actually performed and the recovered data checked, with the observed time set against the tolerable loss window.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
