Obtain the signed coverage schedule of stores, loss windows, retention periods and documented omissions.
Collect backup job configurations and a period of run reports for every protected store.
Gather catalogue entries showing where each copy landed, which credentials can alter it, and the encryption in force.
Request the restore and response-plan exercise record with its date, participants and observed outcome.

Analysis:
Reconcile the coverage schedule against the personal data inventory to find stores neither copied nor deliberately exempted.
Read run reports for failed, skipped or truncated runs and check each was raised rather than superseded silently.
Test the separation of backup credentials from production ones, confirming a compromised production account cannot reach the copies.
Compare restore duration and data completeness observed in the exercise against the loss window the schedule promises.

Output:
A coverage finding naming personal data stores with no backup and no recorded exemption.
A run-success summary per store, with each failure and its follow-up.
An assessment of copy immutability and of credential separation from production.
Measured restore outcomes set beside the agreed tolerable loss windows.

title.en: Decide which data sets are backed up and how much loss each can absorb

description.en: A backup regime inherited from whoever built each system copies what was convenient to copy, not what the organisation could not operate without, and the gap only surfaces during an outage. Name every store holding personal data, state the largest gap between the last usable copy and the moment of failure that the business will accept for it, and state how long copies are held before they expire — a copy retained longer than the data's own retention period quietly reintroduces records that were supposed to be gone. Where a store is deliberately left uncopied, say what would rebuild it and why that is acceptable, so an uncovered store is a decision on the record rather than a discovery made at the worst moment.

evidenceHint.en: Signed coverage schedule listing every store holding personal data, its tolerable loss window, its copy retention period, and the stores deliberately left uncopied with the reason each is safe to omit.

title.en: Schedule each backup and store the copy where production cannot delete it

description.en: A copy that sits in the same account, under the same credentials and on the same storage as the system it protects dies with it: ransomware, a mistaken drop or a lapsed subscription takes both at once. Run each backup at the frequency its agreed loss window demands, write the copy somewhere production's own credentials can neither alter nor delete, and encrypt it, because a backup is the same personal data held in a location with fewer eyes on it. Wire every run's success or failure into somewhere a named person actually reads, and keep a catalogue of which copy of which store sits where — a copy nobody can locate is not a backup, and a job failing silently for weeks is worse than no job at all, because it was believed.

evidenceHint.en: Job configuration plus a period of run reports for every protected store, with the catalogue entry showing where each copy landed, which credentials can alter it, and the encryption applied.

title.en: Exercise a restore and a response plan and record what the exercise showed

description.en: Restore information from backup and rehearse one response or recovery plan end to end, recording what worked, what did not, how long each took, and the improvements agreed with their owners. Share what the exercise showed about how well the protections held with the parties that rely on them, and record who was told.

evidenceHint.en: Exercise record naming what was restored or rehearsed, the date, the participants, the observed outcome, the improvements agreed, and who the findings were shared with.

templates.title: Physical operating environment for assets
templates.description: Implements PR.PO-P4: Policy and regulations regarding the physical operating environment for organizational assets are met.
templates.objective: To ensure spaces holding equipment meet the fire, power and environmental obligations that bind them, proven by exercising the protection rather than reading a certificate.
templates.successCriteria:
Every space housing equipment is scheduled with the statute, lease clause or contract term that binds it and the party answerable for meeting it.
Each space carries recorded power, temperature and fire-suppression figures traceable to the code clause or contract term that sets them.
A contact is named per space who can be reached out of hours when an environmental alarm fires.
Walks exercise the protection by load transfer or suppression activation, and excursions logged since the previous walk are reviewed.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the schedule of equipment spaces with the obligation and the answerable party recorded against each.
Collect the per-space environmental and electrical limit sheets together with the sources they cite.
Gather the dated walk records naming what was loaded or triggered and the result observed.
Request the environmental excursion log covering the interval since the previous walk.

Analysis:
Compare the space schedule against the asset register to find equipment sited somewhere the schedule does not list.
Trace a sample of recorded figures to the code clause, lease term or manufacturer rating claimed as their source.
Confirm the walk exercised generator load transfer, suppression release and the alarm path, rather than inspecting certificates.
Match each logged excursion to a response and check failures carry a named owner and a closure date.

Output:
A schedule of equipment spaces with their governing obligations and any unmapped space named.
A verification note on figures traced to source, naming those resting on none.
Walk-test results per space measured against the limits set for it.
An excursion register showing response status and the owner of each failure.

title.en: Settle which fire, power and building rules bind each space housing equipment

description.en: Obligations over a machine room arrive from three unrelated places — statute and building code, the lease or colocation contract, and the insurer — and none of the three lists the other two. For every space where the organisation's equipment physically sits, including a cage in someone else's data centre and the comms cupboard on a leased floor, name the source of each obligation and the party answerable for meeting it. The usual gap is the space both sides assume the other holds: the tenant reads fire and power as the landlord's business, the landlord sold floor area and nothing more.

evidenceHint.en: Schedule of every space holding equipment, with the statute, lease clause or contract term attached to each and the answerable party named beside it.

title.en: Fix the power, temperature and fire-suppression limits each equipment space must hold

description.en: A room satisfies its rules only at stated numbers: the temperature and humidity band the hardware is warranted in, how many minutes the battery carries the real load, how long the generator runs on the fuel actually on site, which suppression agent is fitted and whether it is safe for a person working in the aisle. Write the figure for each space and, where a site operator supplies it, take the contracted figure rather than the one quoted in a sales pack. State where every alarm lands and who is on the other end at three in the morning, because a threshold nobody is told about is not a threshold.

evidenceHint.en: Per-space sheet giving each environmental and electrical figure in force, its source in the code or the contract, and the person the alarm reaches out of hours.

title.en: Walk each space and test the power and fire protection rather than the certificate

description.en: A service label says a system was installed and inspected; it does not say the heat alarm reaches someone who acts, that the battery carries the true load for the minutes claimed, or that the generator runs beyond the few seconds of a start test. Put each protection under load once in the period, and read the site's own log of what happened since the last pass — heat alarms, supply failures, water on the floor — against the figures set for that space. Where the space belongs to another party, ask what its report actually covered, since a building-wide inspection often stops at the shell and never enters your cage. Anything that failed leaves with a named owner and a date instead of waiting for the next annual visit.

evidenceHint.en: Dated walk record per space naming what was loaded or triggered, the result against the figure set, every excursion logged since the last pass, and the owner of each failure.

templates.title: Improvement of protection processes
templates.description: Implements PR.PO-P5: Protection processes are improved.
templates.objective: To ensure a safeguard that failed is itself changed rather than only the incident it allowed being closed, and that the change reaches the systems it was meant to protect.
templates.successCriteria:
Each failed safeguard has a change record naming the shortfall, what now differs in the mechanism, and the date it took effect.
Agreed improvements are tracked to deployment, with the systems they run on named and overdue items explained.
Repeat failures of the same safeguard are counted, each explained by whether the earlier change landed or failed to hold.
Improvements are drawn from exercises and monitoring results as well as incidents, not from case closure alone.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the change records raised against safeguards that failed during the period.
Collect the improvement status list showing state and deployment scope for each item.
Gather the repeat-failure analysis grouping the period's shortfalls by safeguard, with a count against each.
Request the incident and exercise outputs that the improvements claim to answer.

Analysis:
Pair each event with the safeguard that failed and check whether a mechanism change, not only case closure, was raised.
Verify deployment claims against the systems named, separating improvements approved from improvements actually in force.
Recount repeat failures from the incident record rather than accepting the grouping as supplied.
Examine each repeat for a verdict distinguishing a change that never deployed from one that deployed and proved insufficient.

Output:
A pairing table of events to safeguard changes, naming the events that produced none.
Deployment status per improvement, with overdue items and the reason given for each.
Repeat-failure counts recomputed by the assessor, per safeguard.
Findings on improvements recorded complete but not observable in the systems they name.

title.en: Amend the protection that let an event through, not only the case it caused

description.en: After a safeguard falls short, almost all of the work that follows repairs the instance — the record is corrected, the access is pulled, the individual is told — and the safeguard goes back into service exactly as it was. Name, for every shortfall, what in the protection itself now differs: the rule, the threshold, the default setting, the manual step an automated one replaced, the permission withdrawn. Adding a line to a runbook asking people to take more care is the cheapest answer on offer and the one most easily defeated the same way twice, so log that as an accepted risk rather than count it as an improvement.

evidenceHint.en: Change record for each failed safeguard naming the shortfall that prompted it, what in the mechanism now differs, and the date it took effect.

title.en: Push each agreed protection improvement into force and flag the ones that stalled

description.en: An improvement agreed in a post-incident meeting but never deployed leaves the exposure exactly where it was, while the minutes make it read as settled. Hold a state against each agreed change and close it only once the altered safeguard is running in the place the failure happened — not when the ticket shuts or the code merges. Name every improvement that slipped its date or was quietly abandoned, with the reason, because that population is where the loop stops without anyone noticing.

evidenceHint.en: Status list per improvement showing the shortfall it answers, its current state, where it is now running, and the reason for anything overdue.

title.en: Count the protections that failed twice and find the improvement that never landed

description.en: A safeguard that falls short a second time is the plainest evidence the loop did not work, and nobody sees it unless this period's failures are set beside the previous period's changes. Group the period's control failures, exercise findings, audit results and near misses by the safeguard each one implicates, then pull out every safeguard appearing more than once. For each repeat, separate the three cases — no change was ever made, a change was made somewhere the failure does not occur, or the change landed and is not sufficient — because a single repeat count hides which of them you are holding.

evidenceHint.en: Repeat-failure analysis grouping the period's shortfalls by safeguard, with a count for each and the verdict on why an earlier fix did not hold.

templates.title: Sharing protection effectiveness
templates.description: Implements PR.PO-P6: Effectiveness of protection technologies is shared.
templates.objective: To ensure what the organisation learns about how well its protection technologies perform reaches the peers and sector bodies that can act on it, without releasing exploitable detail.
templates.successCriteria:
Each released account states the conditions the effectiveness was measured under, so a recipient can judge whether it transfers to their own estate.
Every account is marked with the recipient tier it is cleared for, and the detail cut before issue is recorded.
Distribution is logged per release with the receiving organisation, its named contact, the version sent and the confirmation returned.
Measurements taken but never released are visible, each carrying the decision that kept it back.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the released effectiveness accounts for each protection technology and their recipient-tier markings.
Collect the record of detail removed from each account before it was issued.
Gather the distribution log with recipients, versions sent, dates issued and confirmations returned.
Request the period sheet listing every effectiveness measurement taken, released or not.

Analysis:
Set a sample of released accounts beside their source measurements to check the figures and stated conditions survived the edit intact.
Confirm the redaction record explains what was cut and why, rather than merely noting that redaction occurred.
Match logged recipients against the tier each account was cleared for, looking for distribution beyond it.
Identify measurements withheld from release and test whether a decision, not an oversight, kept them back.

Output:
A concordance of released accounts against the measurements behind them.
A finding on accounts issued beyond the recipient tier they were cleared for.
Confirmation status per receiving organisation across the period's releases.
A list of measurements never shared, with the recorded rationale or its absence.

title.en: Package each protection technology's measured effectiveness for the peers and sector bodies receiving it

description.en: An effectiveness result written in the measuring team's own shorthand does not travel: a peer reading it cannot tell what the technology was guarding, at what scale, or which version behaved that way, so a real finding lands as an anecdote and changes nothing at the other end. Write each account with the conditions the measurement was taken under and the failures alongside the successes, then apply a release rule before it leaves — still-open weaknesses and configuration specifics come out, because the same paragraph that helps a peer harden their deployment tells an attacker where yours is thin. Name who signs off a release and which class of recipient, from a sibling engineering team to a sector information-sharing body or a supervisory authority, each version of the account is cleared for.

evidenceHint.en: Released account for each protection technology, marked with the recipient tier it is cleared for, listing the measurement conditions it carries and the detail cut before issue.

title.en: Send each effectiveness account to its named recipients and record who confirmed it arrived

description.en: A distribution list is not a recipient: contacts go stale, a sector body rotates its secretariat, and a report can sit unopened for a quarter while the organisation believes the exchange happened. Log the receiving organisation, the person who confirmed it arrived, the version sent and the date, so a later question about whether a finding was passed on is answerable from the record rather than from anyone's memory. Return traffic is part of the same task — a peer asking how the measurement was taken is owed a reply, and one unanswered question quietly ends the exchange for good.

evidenceHint.en: Distribution log per release: receiving organisation, named contact, version sent, date issued, and the confirmation returned.

title.en: Compare the accounts recipients received against the effectiveness results actually measured

description.en: Two defects hide here and neither shows up in the sending log. The first is silence: a protection technology whose effectiveness was measured and then reported to nobody outside the team, which surfaces only when the period's measurements are used as the denominator and each one is checked for a release. The second is the flattering account — the failure that was in the measurement and is not in what the recipient read, because redaction and reputational instinct delete the same paragraph. Read a sample of issued accounts beside their source results and name what went missing on the way out.

evidenceHint.en: Period sheet listing every effectiveness measurement taken, whether it was released and to whom, plus a sampled account set beside its source result with the omissions named.

templates.title: Response and recovery plans
templates.description: Implements PR.PO-P7: Response plans (Incident Response and Business Continuity) and recovery plans (Incident Recovery and Disaster Recovery) are established, in place, and managed.
templates.objective: To ensure a named and current plan stands ready for each disruption and privacy event the organisation could face, with every step owned and the handover into recovery settled in advance.
templates.successCriteria:
A coverage matrix maps each in-scope scenario to the plan that answers it and names the scenarios deliberately left uncovered.
Each plan fixes the point where handling passes from containment to the return of normal service, and who owns either side of it.
Every plan step names an executor by role, with a deputy or escalation where that role rests on one person.
Roles, contacts, suppliers and dependencies cited across the plans still resolve when checked, and corrections issue where they do not.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the scenario coverage matrix and the plan documents it points to.
Collect the current response and recovery plans with their step-level role assignments.
Gather the dated reference check covering roles, contacts, suppliers and dependencies named across the plans.
Request the corrections issued wherever a cited reference failed to resolve.

Analysis:
Compare the scenario list against the risk register and recent events to find disruptions no plan addresses.
Follow one plan end to end and confirm the containment-to-recovery handover is stated, not merely implied by document order.
Sample cited contacts and supplier arrangements and test independently whether each still exists and remains in force.
Check plan steps for executors who have left, or for roles now vacant, with no deputy named behind them.

Output:
A coverage matrix annotated with the scenarios holding no plan.
A handover finding per plan, naming those where the transition point is undefined.
Reference-check results giving the proportion of citations that failed to resolve.
A list of plan steps with no executable owner as at the date of test.

title.en: Map each disruption and privacy event to the plan that must answer it

description.en: Fix the list of events the organisation must be able to answer — an outage, a supplier collapsing, a ransomware demand, personal data reaching somewhere it should not — and say which document carries each one, from the first hour through to the return of normal service. What falls through is the seam between documents: a privacy event no security incident document claims as its own, or a failure whose handling is clearly owned while each document assumes the other brings the service back. Write down the events deliberately left without a plan as well, so a later gap reads as a decision on the record rather than an omission nobody noticed.

evidenceHint.en: Coverage matrix naming every scenario in scope, the document that carries it, the point where handling passes from containment to the return of normal service, and the scenarios deliberately left uncovered.

title.en: Record the response and recovery plans and who executes each step

description.en: Capture the plans for responding to an incident, continuing the business through it, and recovering afterwards; for each plan record the steps in order, the person accountable for each, and the systems and data each step depends on. Name what each plan assumes is still available, since that assumption is what the exercise later tests.

title.en: Find the plan steps whose named executor, contact or system no longer exists

description.en: A plan rots by reference: the named deputy left in March, the escalation number rings a disconnected desk, the supplier was swapped at renewal, and the standby system a step says to switch to was decommissioned last year. Walk the plans line by line against the current roster, the contact directory, the supplier register and the system inventory, and mark every reference that no longer resolves to a real person, number or asset. Reissue each plan with the corrections and a fresh approval date instead of leaving the findings in a review note, because the copy someone opens at three in the morning is the published one.

evidenceHint.en: Dated reference check listing every role, contact detail, supplier and dependency named across the plans, whether each still resolves today, and the correction issued where it did not.

templates.title: Exercising response and recovery plans
templates.description: Implements PR.PO-P8: Response and recovery plans are tested.
templates.objective: To ensure the plans are rehearsed under time pressure by the people who would execute them, so the decisions and hand-offs that fail are discovered before a real event forces them.
templates.successCriteria:
An approved programme names each scenario to be rehearsed in the period, its format, the participants required to attend, and the decisions it must force.
Each exercise runs to a scripted inject timeline, with halt criteria agreed before play begins.
Observers mark against a prepared scoring grid rather than composing a narrative after the event.
The exercise log records decisions reached or missed against the clock, every failed hand-off, and each plan contact who did not answer.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the approved exercise programme for the period with the participants required per scenario.
Collect the scenario packs holding the timed inject lists, scoring grids and agreed halt criteria.
Gather the dated exercise logs with clock times recorded against each decision point.
Request the attendance records for the exercises actually held.

Analysis:
Compare the exercises run against the approved programme to find scenarios deferred or quietly dropped.
Check attendance against the required-participant list, noting decision-holders who sent a delegate instead.
Confirm the halt criteria and scoring grid predate play, rather than being written to fit what occurred.
Read the logs for stalled decisions, failed hand-offs and unreachable contacts, and trace each to a plan amendment.

Output:
A delivery record for the programme, naming the scenarios never exercised.
Participation findings per exercise measured against the required roster.
Timed decision outcomes drawn from the exercise logs.
Exercise observations set beside the plan changes they produced, and those that produced none.

title.en: Choose which scenarios go to rehearsal and who must be in the room

description.en: A plan is only ever exercised against situations somebody picked in advance, so the picking is the control: name the scenarios for the period, the form each one takes — a seated walkthrough, an out-of-hours call-out with no warning, a hand-over that crosses a shift boundary — and the people whose absence would make the result meaningless. Put the deputies and the outside parties the plan relies on into that list, because a rehearsal that only ever assembles the willing and the available proves nothing about a Sunday morning. State what each scenario has to demonstrate before it counts as attempted: which decisions have to be reached, by whom, and inside what elapsed time.

evidenceHint.en: Approved exercise programme for the period listing each scenario, its format, the participants required to attend, and the decisions it must produce.

title.en: Script the injects, the clock and the observer's marking sheet

description.en: An exercise that hands everyone the whole story at the start tests reading comprehension, not judgement under pressure. Break each scenario into timed injects that arrive the way facts really arrive — partial, contradictory, out of order — and fix beforehand the moments where a decision, an escalation or a hand-off is expected, since those moments are the thing being measured. Give observers a grid that marks each one made, missed or deferred with the time it happened, and agree the halt criteria that let the director stop the game before it touches live service or a real customer.

evidenceHint.en: Scenario pack containing the timed inject list, the scoring grid each observer marks against, and the halt criteria agreed before play.

title.en: Run the rehearsal and log every stalled decision, hand-off and unreachable contact

description.en: Capture what the participants actually did rather than what the plan says they should have done: which decision stalled and on what missing fact, which hand-off fell between two roles who each assumed the other had it, and which name in the plan nobody could raise. Contact details rot quietly, so a number that went to voicemail is a finding in its own right, and so is a deputy who had never been told they were one. Write it down while the room is still assembled — a gap recorded the same hour is a defect with an owner, and the same gap reconstructed a week later is only an anecdote.

evidenceHint.en: Dated log of the exercise naming each decision reached or missed with its clock time, every failed hand-off, and each plan contact who did not answer.

templates.title: Privacy in human resources practice
templates.description: Implements PR.PO-P9: Privacy procedures are included in human resources practices (e.g., deprovisioning, personnel screening).
templates.objective: To ensure the people process itself screens a post to the data it can reach, and moves access with the person as they join, change role and leave.
templates.successCriteria:
Every post carries a screening grade set by what it can read, export or act upon, and that grade's vetting cleared before the start date.
The hiring, role-change and departure procedures name the privacy steps owed and who performs each, binding agency, contract and seconded workers too.
A move into a grade of wider reach triggers the re-check that grade requires.
Starters, movers and leavers taken from the HR record had their owed steps done on or before the effective date.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the screening standard showing each grade of post, the vetting owed before a start date, and the worker types it binds.
Collect the amended hiring, role-change and departure procedures with their privacy steps and named performers.
Draw the period's starters, movers and leavers from payroll or the HR record rather than from the requests departures generated.
Retrieve the vetting files, data-holding hand-backs and confidentiality restatements for the sampled names.

Analysis:
Confirm each sampled post's grade reflects the data it can reach and that vetting cleared before the first day worked.
Establish for each mover and leaver the date access was withdrawn and holdings returned, and measure it against the effective date.
Test whether agency assignments that simply ended and moves filed as transfers still produced the steps they owed.
Identify names present in payroll but absent from the request-driven population.

Output:
Starter, mover and leaver comparison showing the steps owed and the date each was performed or found missing.
Schedule of posts whose screening grade understates the data reach of the post.
List of steps performed after the effective date, each raised as a finding in its own right.

title.en: Grade each post by the data it will touch and fix the screening each grade requires

description.en: Screening pitched at seniority rather than at data reach leaves a junior post holding whole customer files unvetted while a director who touches nothing is checked twice over. Set the grade from what the post can actually read, export or act upon, and state what each grade must clear before a start date, including references, employment history, and any criminal-record check the law permits. Say plainly which worker types the standard binds, because agency staff, contractors, interns and secondees are never formally hired and so fall outside a rule drafted for employees. Name the re-check owed when somebody moves up into a grade with wider reach than the one they were vetted for.

evidenceHint.en: Screening standard listing every grade of post, the vetting owed before a start date, and the worker types it binds, including agency and contract staff.

title.en: Record the privacy steps in hiring, role change and departure

description.en: For joining, moving and leaving, state what must happen to the person's access, to the data they hold, and to any checks made about them before they are trusted with data, and name who performs each step. Attach the amended people process rather than a separate privacy leaflet beside it.

title.en: Draw the period's starters, movers and leavers from payroll, then test the people process against that list

description.en: The exits that go wrong are the ones nobody raised a request for: an agency assignment that simply ended, an internal move filed as a transfer so nothing was withdrawn, a last day that shifted after the paperwork went in. Taking the population from payroll or the HR record rather than from the requests the departures generated gives a denominator the process cannot quietly shrink. For each name, check that the screening the post required was complete before the start date and that the leaving or moving steps happened, from data holdings returned or handed over through to the confidentiality obligation being restated. Treat a step performed weeks after the effective date as a finding of its own rather than a closed item.

evidenceHint.en: Period comparison naming everyone who joined, changed role or left according to the HR record, the privacy steps owed for each, and the date each was carried out or found missing.

templates.title: Vulnerability management plan
templates.description: Implements PR.PO-P10: A vulnerability management plan is developed and implemented.
templates.objective: To ensure weaknesses in what the organisation runs are rated and owned on arrival, repaired inside the deadline it set itself, and proven gone once signed off.
templates.successCriteria:
The plan names where findings arrive from, how they are ranked, who repairs them, and who accepts one nobody will fix.
Every register entry carries an origin, rating, owner and repair date from intake, so a late item is distinguishable from an open one.
Items past their repair date have been escalated, and a compensating measure has not closed the underlying weakness.
Verification postdates the sign-off it tests, and anything answering again re-enters the queue on a fresh deadline.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the vulnerability management plan with its intake sources, ranking scheme, repair deadlines and acceptance authority.
Export the finding register for the period showing origin, rating, owner, deadline, current state and every escalation raised.
Collect the verification runs, each dated after the closures it re-examines.
Gather the acceptance records for weaknesses left unrepaired and the compensating measures logged beside them.

Analysis:
Count entries admitted with no rating, owner or repair date, since an item without a date cannot be shown to be late.
Set each overdue entry beside the escalation raised for it and note the ones carrying none.
Check that mitigated entries stayed open on the underlying weakness's own clock rather than being marked done.
Match the verification results against the sign-offs they postdate and count the closures contradicted.
Confirm a weakness that answered again was raised as a new item rather than reopened quietly on the old deadline.

Output:
Ageing of the finding register against the organisation's own repair deadlines.
Schedule of sign-offs the verification run contradicted, with the disposal recorded for each.
Register of accepted weaknesses naming the person who accepted each.

title.en: Write the vulnerability management plan and name who acts on each source of findings

description.en: State where the organisation learns about weaknesses in what it runs, how a finding is triaged and ranked, who fixes it, and within what the organisation itself sets. Record what happens to a finding nobody will fix, and who accepts it.

title.en: Triage each incoming vulnerability and escalate the ones past their fix date

description.en: Findings arrive from scanners, vendor advisories, penetration tests and outside reporters at different rates, and every one needs a rating and a repair date before it joins the queue. Where no date is attached at intake, an item that is merely open cannot be told apart from one that is late, so the queue can be reported only as a size rather than as a breach of what the organisation promised itself. Where a compensating measure goes in instead of a repair, leave the underlying weakness open on its own clock, since a mitigated entry marked done disappears from view while the exposure is still there.

evidenceHint.en: Export of the finding register for the period listing origin, rating, owner, deadline, current state and the escalation raised for anything late.

title.en: Re-scan the systems where a fix was signed off and list what comes back

description.en: A closed ticket proves the work was done, not that the weakness is gone: the rebuilt image may not be the one running, a library can be pinned in the manifest and still loaded from an older path, and a redeployment can restore the very version that was taken out. Run the check against the live system rather than a branch or a staging copy, and count how many sign-offs it contradicts. Anything that answers again returns to the queue as a fresh item with its own deadline, rather than being reopened quietly against the old one.

evidenceHint.en: Verification run dated after the closures it tests, naming each item re-examined, the result, and how any contradiction was dealt with.

templates.title: Issue, revocation and audit of credentials
templates.description: Implements PR.AC-P1: Identities and credentials are issued, managed, verified, revoked, and audited for authorized individuals, processes, and devices.
templates.objective: To ensure every credential against a data-processing system was authorised at issue, traceable through its changes, and actually stopped working when the event requiring its end occurred.
templates.successCriteria:
Each system in the inventory records who and what holds credentials to it and the role that authorised each grant.
The procedure states what is established before issue, the strength each class of transaction demands, and the events compelling revocation within a stated limit.
An ended credential reconstructs from the systems themselves: authorising entry, intervening changes, triggering event and the moment access ceased.
Credentials nobody can account for stand as findings, not silent deletions.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the per-system list of credentialed individuals, processes and devices with the authorising role named against each grant.
Collect the procedure covering the whole life of a credential, issue, proof, change and revocation.
Draw a sample of credentials the directories and applications themselves show as ended in the period, not from closure records.
Retrieve directory change history, application logs and the last successful authentication for each sampled credential.

Analysis:
Reconstruct each sampled credential's life and fix its authorising entry, every change it passed through and the event that should have ended it.
Measure the gap between that triggering event and the timestamp access genuinely ceased against the organisation's own stated limit.
Mark entries surviving only as a closure ticket, where the revocation happened but can no longer be evidenced.
Compare the holder record with live grants to surface credentials no authorising role stands behind.

Output:
Sample schedule of ended credentials carrying authorising record, triggering event, cessation timestamp and elapsed gap.
List of revocations evidenced by a ticket alone.
Register of unaccounted credentials raised as findings, with the system each sits on.

title.en: Record who and what holds credentials to each data-processing system

description.en: Per system in the inventory, list the individuals, processes and devices holding credentials to it, and name the role that authorises each grant. Record credentials that nobody can account for as findings rather than deleting them silently.

title.en: Define how a credential is issued, proved, changed and revoked

description.en: State what must be established about a person or device before a credential is issued to it, how strongly a request must be authenticated for each class of transaction the system carries, and what events require a credential to be revoked and within what the organisation itself sets. Attach the procedure covering the whole life of a credential, not only its issue.

title.en: Reconstruct a revoked credential's life from the systems, not the closure ticket

description.en: Revocation destroys its own evidence: deleting an account takes with it who authorised the credential, what it was changed to mid-life, and the moment it actually stopped working, leaving only a ticket asserting the job was done. Draw the sample from credentials the directories and applications themselves show as ended in the period rather than from closure records, and for each one establish the authorising entry, every change it passed through, the event that should have ended it, and the timestamp access genuinely ceased. A revocation that happened but can no longer be evidenced is a finding in its own right, as is a credential that outlived its triggering event by longer than the organisation's own stated limit.

evidenceHint.en: Sample of ended credentials with, per entry, the authorising record, the changes in between, the triggering event, the date access actually ceased, the elapsed gap, and the entries where only a ticket survives.

templates.title: Physical access to data and devices
templates.description: Implements PR.AC-P2: Physical access to data and devices is managed.
templates.objective: To ensure nobody comes within touching distance of a record or a machine processing data without meeting a barrier that halts them, wherever that data physically sits.
templates.successCriteria:
The scoping sheet covers every site, enclosure and carried device putting a person within reach of data, and names who settled the borderline cases.
Assets that travel are scoped by the person holding them rather than by a fixed address.
Each location records what limits entry, who authorises one and what is kept about entries, including locations another party runs for the organisation.
An unbadged, unannounced approach is halted short of the data, and the entry record shows the visit.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the scoping sheet listing sites, enclosures and mobile assets, the in-or-out test applied and the borderline settlements.
Collect the entry limits, authorising roles and entry records held for each in-scope location.
Gather what is known about locations run by another party, including shared cages and racks.
Retrieve the dated attempt sheet from the unannounced approach and the entry records covering that day.

Analysis:
Test the scoping sheet against the processing inventory for filing cabinets of signed forms, printer output trays and laptops that go home.
Follow the attempted route and fix the point at which a lock or a human being actually halted it, not the point policy predicts.
Compare the attempt against the entry record to establish whether the visit was captured at all.
Assess whether each travelling asset is tied to a named holder rather than to a location.

Output:
Findings from the unannounced approach naming the route tried, the halting point and what failed to stop it.
Gap list of data-holding places absent from the scoping sheet.
Statement of third-party-operated locations and what the organisation can evidence about each.

title.en: Locate every room, cabinet and carried device that puts a person within reach of data

description.en: Physical scoping usually stops at the server room and misses where data actually sits: a filing cabinet of signed forms, a printer's output tray, a laptop that goes home each night, a rack in a cage shared with other tenants. Name each site, enclosure and mobile asset that brings a human being within touching distance of data or of a machine processing it, and state the test that decides whether something falls in or out. Assets that travel have no fixed address, so scope those by who holds them rather than by where they sit.

evidenceHint.en: Scoping sheet listing each site, enclosure and mobile asset in scope, the in-or-out test applied, and the borderline cases settled with who settled them.

title.en: Record how physical access to data and devices is controlled

description.en: For each location holding data or devices that process it, record what limits who may enter, who authorises an entry, and what is recorded about entries that happen. Include locations operated by another party on the organisation's behalf and what is known about them.

title.en: Reach a device holding data without presenting a credential, and note where you were stopped

description.en: Barriers fail on the routes nobody issued: a door propped open for a delivery, a cabinet whose key hangs on the wall beside it, a lobby that admits anyone carrying a coffee, another tenant's engineer passing your rack on the way to theirs. Send someone with no badge and no appointment to get within touching distance of a machine or a stored record, and write down the point at which a lock or a human being actually halted them, rather than the point where policy says they would have been halted. If nothing halted them at all, that absence is the finding, and an entry log showing no visit is a second one.

evidenceHint.en: Dated attempt sheet naming the route tried, the point at which the attempt was halted, by whom or what, and the findings raised from it.

templates.title: Remote access
templates.description: Implements PR.AC-P3: Remote access is managed.
templates.objective: To ensure each connection reaching the organisation's systems from off its premises belongs to a named way of working and to a worker that arrangement still covers.
templates.successCriteria:
The scoping note names each off-site way of working in scope, the groups working that way, the systems needed from there, and the exclusions with who settled them.
Vendor dial-in for maintenance sits deliberately outside this scope and is managed where maintenance is.
Every route in from outside has an owner and stated requirements on its users; a route existing without one is recorded as such.
Sessions in the period each trace back to a covered worker and a sanctioned way in.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the scoping note covering home working, travel, client and partner desks and personal devices, with groups and systems named against each.
Collect the register of routes into the network from outside, their owners and what is required of their users.
Export the period's connection records from the concentrators, gateways and identity provider.
Gather engagement end dates, sanctioned working countries and the record of ways in opened for a single piece of work.

Analysis:
Work outward from the connection records and attribute every session to an opener, an off-site situation and a route.
Count sessions with no covered worker or no sanctioned way in behind them, the plainly innocent ones included.
Look for connections raised after an engagement ended, from an unsanctioned country, or over a way in never shut.
Identify routes appearing in the connection data but missing from the route register.

Output:
Period trace naming the records examined, the sessions they held and those that could not be attributed.
List of routes standing without an owner, raised against a named recipient.
Record of what was done about each unattributed session.

title.en: Name the off-site working situations that count as remote access

description.en: Settle which ways of working away from the organisation's own premises are in scope here — home working, travel, a desk at a client or partner site, a personal phone used for evening messages — and name the staff, contractors and on-call groups that work each way, together with the systems holding personal data each needs to get at from there. A situation nobody named is the one that ends up managed by nobody, and later checks have no population to measure against. A vendor engineer dialling in to service an asset is deliberately out of scope: that sits with maintenance, and mixing the two leaves ordinary remote working judged against rules written for someone else.

evidenceHint.en: Scoping note listing each way of working away from the premises that is in scope, the groups that work that way, the systems they need from there, and the exclusions with the person who settled them.

title.en: Record how systems are reached from outside and how the network is kept separated

description.en: List the routes by which systems can be reached from outside the organisation's own network, who may use each and what is required of them, and record how the parts of the network holding data are kept apart from the parts that have no need of it. Record every route that exists without an owner.

title.en: Trace each connection from outside back to a remote worker the arrangement covers

description.en: Work from the connection records for the period rather than the list of approved remote workers, and account for every session: who opened it, the off-site working situation that entitles them to it, and the way in they used. This arrangement decays through changed circumstances rather than bad decisions — an engagement that ended, a move to a country nobody sanctioned, a way in opened for one trip and never shut — and none of that appears in a register only ever read forwards. Treat a session that cannot be tied to a covered worker as a finding even where it was plainly innocent, because the same gap would carry someone who was not.

evidenceHint.en: Period trace naming the records examined, how many sessions they held, each one with no covered worker or sanctioned way in behind it, and what was done about it.

templates.title: Least privilege and separation of duties
templates.description: Implements PR.AC-P4: Access permissions and authorizations are managed, incorporating the principles of least privilege and separation of duties.
templates.objective: To ensure no single holder carries reach beyond what their role needs, and that duties required to stay apart genuinely rest in two different pairs of hands.
templates.successCriteria:
Each system's grantable permission sets are banded by what one holder could reach, alter, export or re-grant alone, and the band line is stated.
Permissions that confer further permissions are banded too, not left outside the scheme.
Every role's permissions carry a reason, the duty pairs that must not meet are named, and each unavoidable overlap is accepted with something compensating for it.
Audit finds recorded holders and permissions matching what each system grants today, with differences corrected or accepted.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the banding table naming each in-scope system, the permission sets it can grant, the band assigned and the reach that justified it.
Collect the role definitions showing permissions held, the reason recorded for each, and the pairs of duties held apart.
Retrieve the acceptances and compensating measures for places separation is not currently possible.
Export today's grants from each system alongside the audit worksheet comparing them with the records.

Analysis:
Check that sets letting a holder widen their own grant were banded rather than left outside the scheme.
Test where the band line sits, who settles a set that straddles it, and whether any system's grants could not be enumerated at all.
Classify each difference between export and record as excess reach, a holder no longer present, or a grant made outside the process.
Confirm each named duty pair is held by two people in the live grants, not merely in the role definitions.

Output:
Reconciliation of recorded permissions against live grants, difference by difference, with the correction or acceptance taken.
Schedule of duty pairs found in one holder's hands and what compensates for each.
List of systems whose grantable permissions could not be enumerated.

title.en: Grade the permissions by what a single holder could do with them

description.en: Take the permission sets each in-scope system can hand out and place each into a band by what it lets one holder reach, alter, export or re-grant without a second person acting. State where the line between bands sits and who settles a set that straddles it, because until that line exists least privilege has no denominator and a later review covers only the grants somebody happened to think of. Include the permissions that confer further permissions, since a holder who can widen their own grant sits outside every band already agreed.

evidenceHint.en: Banding table naming each in-scope system, the permission sets it can grant, the band assigned to each, the reach that justified that band, and any system whose grants could not be enumerated.

title.en: Record the permissions each role holds and the duties held apart

description.en: For every role, record the permissions granted to it, why the role needs each of them, and which pairs of duties must not rest with the same person. Record the places where separation is not currently possible, with who accepted that and what compensates for it.

title.en: Audit the credential and permission records against what the systems actually grant

description.en: Compare the recorded holders and permissions against what each system grants today, one system at a time, and record every difference — an account with more than its role, a holder no longer present, a permission granted outside the process. Record the correction made or the acceptance taken for each difference.

evidenceHint.en: Audit worksheet naming the systems compared, each difference found between record and grant, and the correction or acceptance recorded against it.

templates.title: Network segregation and segmentation
templates.description: Implements PR.AC-P5: Network integrity is protected (e.g., network segregation, network segmentation).
templates.objective: To ensure zones holding data are joined only by crossings somebody owns and renews, and that nothing outside the rule set quietly carries traffic between them.
templates.successCriteria:
Every processing system in the inventory sits in a named zone with a stated trust level, and hosts fitting no zone are listed with an owner.
Each permitted crossing names its origin and destination zones, service, owner and lapse date, with everything unlisted refused by default.
Crossings already in place with nobody behind them appear as open items rather than being grandfathered in silence.
Connections the register says are impossible do not complete when attempted from a machine inside each zone.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the segment register listing zones, trust levels, the processing systems assigned to each and the hosts that could not be placed.
Collect the rule register with origin and destination zones, service carried, accountable owner, lapse date and the default-deny position.
Retrieve routing tables, interface listings, cloud peering configuration and management VLAN membership.
Gather the dated test log from connections attempted out of a machine in each zone.

Analysis:
Build zone assignment from the systems inventory outward and set it against the diagram to find machines plugged in afterwards.
Count rules carrying no owner or no lapse date, and those whose justifying migration or support session has ended.
Set every attempted connection's observed response beside the outcome the register predicted.
For each unexplained success, trace the static route, dual-homed host, peering or flat management network carrying it.

Output:
Test log of attempted crossings giving originating machine, target service, predicted outcome and observed response.
List of paths joining zones outside the rule set, naming the component carrying each.
Register of unplaceable hosts and of rules standing without an owner.

title.en: Name each network segment and the systems it is allowed to admit

description.en: Segregation is only a claim until every system that processes data sits in a named segment with a stated level of trust, so set out the segments, what each one may hold, and the rule that decides where a newly built system goes. Build the list from the systems in the inventory outward rather than from the network diagram, because the diagram shows the design and not the machines that were plugged in afterwards. A host that fits no segment — a supplier's box sharing a subnet with a data store, an appliance homed on two networks at once — is exactly what this step is meant to surface.

evidenceHint.en: Segment register listing every zone, its trust level, the processing systems assigned to it, and each host that could not be placed, with an owner named against it.

title.en: Tie each permitted crossing to a source, a destination, an owner and a date it lapses

description.en: A segmentation rule set decays by accretion: an allowance opened for a migration or a vendor's support session outlives the work that justified it, and two zones end up joined in fact while the diagram still shows them apart. Write every permitted crossing as a row naming the originating zone, the zone it reaches, the service it carries, the person accountable, and the date it falls away unless somebody renews it; traffic outside that list is refused by default rather than tolerated. Rules already in place with nobody behind them belong on the same list as open items, not grandfathered in silence.

evidenceHint.en: Rule register showing, per entry, the originating and destination zones, the service allowed, the accountable owner, the renewal or lapse date, and the default-deny position covering everything unlisted.

title.en: Attempt the crossings the rules forbid from a host inside each segment

description.en: Reading the rule table proves what was intended, not what the running network does: a forgotten static route, a host homed on two segments, a cloud peering or a flat management VLAN can join two zones that no rule mentions. Work from inside — from a machine in each segment, try to open the connections the register says are impossible, including those between zones that never needed to speak — and note for every attempt what answered. A connection that completes where the register denies it is a defect even though no rule permits it, because something outside the rule set is carrying the traffic, and the fix belongs there rather than in another rule.

evidenceHint.en: Dated test log naming the originating machine, the target address and service, the outcome the register predicted, the response observed, and each unexplained success with the path found to be carrying it.

templates.title: Identity proofing and authentication strength
templates.description: Implements PR.AC-P6: Individuals and devices are proofed and bound to credentials, and authenticated commensurate with the risk of the transaction.
templates.objective: To ensure a credential is bound only to a claimant proved to a stated bar, and that the acts able to do most harm demand stronger or fresher authentication than the login did.
templates.successCriteria:
The enrolment standard names the identity evidence acceptable per class of holder, contractors, service accounts and devices alike.
Weaker evidence is accepted only by a named authority and leaves behind what that decision must.
Acts above the risk line are listed per system with the assurance enforced and the layer running it, that layer being the service, not the interface.
A credential enrolled at the lowest bar completes no high-risk act by any route, API, mobile client and recovery path included.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the enrolment standard giving acceptable identity evidence per class of holder and the authority able to accept less.
Collect the per-system list of acts classed above the risk line, the assurance level enforced at each and the layer running that check.
Draw a sample of bindings made in the period together with the identity evidence actually held for each holder.
Retrieve the dated test log from driving a lowest-bar credential at the high-risk acts.

Analysis:
Compare the evidence held for each sampled binding against the bar in force on the day the credential was bound.
Drive the high-risk acts through the API, a mobile client and every recovery path, recording the assurance the credential held and the outcome.
Establish whether a step-up is enforced at the endpoint that performs the act or only in the interface that offers it.
Determine where re-authentication is compelled mid-session and where one weak authentication rides along into later acts.

Output:
Test log naming each act reached, the route it was reached by, the credential's assurance and the result.
Binding sample setting the evidence found beside the bar that applied on the day.
List of decisions accepting weaker evidence with the authority behind each.

title.en: Set the proof of identity required before a credential is bound

description.en: State what evidence establishes that a claimant really is the person or device they say they are — documents checked back to their issuer, a live or in-person check, an existing credential of known strength, a hardware attestation or a certificate for a machine — and set a different bar for each class of holder, including contractors, service accounts and devices. Without a stated bar, enrolment quietly settles for whatever the requester could produce that day, and the credential carries an assurance nobody can state afterwards. Name who may accept weaker evidence and what such a decision must leave behind, because those are the holders who later turn out to have the most reach.

evidenceHint.en: The enrolment standard naming acceptable identity evidence per class of holder, with the authority to accept weaker evidence and what that decision must leave behind.

title.en: Step up the authentication strength as a transaction's risk rises

description.en: Sort the acts each system offers by what a wrongly authenticated actor could do with them — reading one record, exporting a whole population, changing a payout destination, altering someone else's data — and require stronger or fresher authentication at the acts above the line instead of only at the start of the session. Authenticate once weakly and that assurance otherwise rides along into every action the session reaches for the rest of the day. Decide where re-authentication is compelled mid-session, and put the check at the service that performs the act rather than in the interface that offers it.

evidenceHint.en: A list of the acts classed above the line in each system, each with the assurance level enforced and the layer where that check runs.

title.en: Attempt the riskiest transaction with the weakest credential that reaches it

description.en: Take a credential enrolled at the lowest bar and drive it at the acts classed as high risk, reaching them through the API, a mobile client and any recovery path as well as the main screen. A step-up that the interface enforces and the endpoint does not will survive every desk-based review and fail this one. Then pull a sample of the bindings made in the period and compare the evidence actually held for each holder against the bar that applied on the day it was bound.

evidenceHint.en: Dated test log naming each act reached, the route it was reached by, the assurance the credential held and the outcome, alongside the sampled bindings and the evidence found for each.

templates.title: Protection of data at rest
templates.description: Implements PR.DS-P1: Data-at-rest are protected.
templates.objective: To ensure stored data stays unreadable to anyone reaching it beneath the application, and that its keys are not returned on request by the very platform holding the data.
templates.successCriteria:
Every store records what protects the data held there, who can lift that protection, and each copy outside production with what separates it.
The per-store listing gives the cipher, the key's custodian and location, the identities entitled to call for it, and its last rotation date.
A store that cannot take encryption carries a compensating measure and a named signed acceptance of the exposure left.
Underlying files, a snapshot and an export read at the storage layer come back illegible.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the per-store record of what protects the data, who can lift it, and every copy of that data outside production.
Collect the cipher in force, key custodian and location, the identities that may call for the key, and the last rotation date for each store.
Retrieve signed acceptances and compensating measures for stores left unprotected.
Gather the dated test note from reads performed with the application out of the path.

Analysis:
Establish whether a key is held by the same platform that would hand it back on request, and which operator, console credential or vendor support path could call for it.
Check that rotation followed the departure of each identity entitled to call for the key.
Open a store's underlying files, one snapshot and one export at the storage layer and record which reads returned legible values.
Set the register's copy list against the replicas, clones and restores actually present.

Output:
Test note naming the artefacts opened, the route used beneath the service and what returned readable.
Per-store key schedule carrying custodian, calling identities and rotation date.
Remediation list covering copies found in the clear and copies nobody had listed.

title.en: Record the protection applied to data at rest in each store

description.en: For every store in the inventory, record what protects the data held there, who is able to lift that protection, and where a copy of the same data exists outside the production environment together with what separates that copy from production. A copy nobody listed is the finding this task exists to surface.

title.en: Encrypt each store in the register and hold its keys elsewhere

description.en: A volume encrypted under a key the same platform will hand back on request defends against a disk carried out of the building and against nothing else: an operator, a leaked console credential and the provider's own support path all still read the values plainly. For every store in the register, settle what encrypts it, where the key sits, which identities may call for the key, and what rotates it when one of those identities departs. Stores that cannot take encryption at all — an ageing appliance, a vendor-run database, a file share nobody owns — need the compensating measure written down and a named person who accepted the exposure that remains.

evidenceHint.en: Per-store listing of the cipher in force, the key's custodian and location, the last rotation date, and a signed acceptance for anything left unprotected.

title.en: Read a store's files and snapshots from beneath the application

description.en: Protection is asserted in a configuration page and lost in practice — a replica cloned before the policy existed, a snapshot restored into a storage class with no key attached, a cipher switched off for a migration and never switched back. Take a store the register calls protected, open its underlying files, one snapshot and one export without the application in the path, and see whether the values come back legible. A test that only re-reads the configuration proves the setting, not the bytes, so record which reads were done at the storage layer and raise every copy that returned in the clear.

evidenceHint.en: Dated test note naming the artefacts opened, the route used to reach them under the service, what returned readable, and the remediation raised for each.

templates.title: Protection of data in transit
templates.description: Implements PR.DS-P2: Data-in-transit are protected.
templates.objective: To ensure a transmission reaches the protection its class demands by refusing anything weaker, and that every point at which a session is opened up is known and accounted for.
templates.successCriteria:
The scoping statement names each class of transmission in scope, internal ones included, with the result a connection must reach and the weaker ones it refuses.
Every hop unwrapping and re-making a session is named, so the intervals where data travels in the clear are known.
Each flow on the processing map records what protects it in motion, the receiving side's obligation, and who agreed it.
Routes whose far end changed were re-checked, and any that fell back and kept working stands open against its owner.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the scoping statement with the classes in scope, the negotiated outcome required and the weaker results a connection must refuse.
Collect the list of proxies, gateways, load balancers and managed inspection points where a session is unwrapped and re-made.
Retrieve the flow-by-flow record of protection, receiving-side obligations and the person who agreed each.
Gather the period's far-end changes from partner and provider notices, deprecation schedules and certificate renewal dates.

Analysis:
Re-check what each affected route now achieves when it connects, instead of carrying last period's recorded value forward.
Identify routes that negotiated down to a weaker result and kept working, with nothing failing and no alert raised.
Confirm flows travelling unprotected appear as open rows with an owner rather than being omitted from the map.
Check the scope acknowledges the clear-text interval at each unwrapping hop instead of treating the next hop as someone else's concern.

Output:
Period review setting each far-end change beside the routes it touched and what those routes now achieve.
List of routes still carrying data at a reduced setting, each with the owner who must close it.
Inventory of unwrapping points and what holds the data at each.

title.en: Fix the protection each transmission must negotiate and where it may be broken open

description.en: Name the classes of transmission in scope, including the ones that never leave the organisation's own network, and for each state the outcome a connection must reach and the weaker result it has to refuse rather than settle for. Protection on the wire is the product of a negotiation between two endpoints, so a standard that names only an acceptable result is satisfied by a connection that quietly agreed to less. Name also the places where a session is unwrapped and re-made — a proxy, a gateway, a load balancer, a managed inspection point — because the data is in the clear at each of them and the scope has to say so rather than assume the hop away.

evidenceHint.en: Scoping statement listing each class of transmission held in scope, the outcome a connection is required to reach, the weaker results it must refuse, and every hop at which a session is unwrapped and re-made.

title.en: Record the protection applied to each data flow between systems

description.en: For every flow on the processing map, record what protects the data while it moves, what the receiving side is required to do to keep it protected, and who agreed that arrangement. Record flows travelling with no protection as open rows with an owner rather than omitting them.

title.en: Re-check the routes whose far endpoint changed since the protection was last agreed

description.en: A route is only ever as well protected as the other end will still accept, so it can weaken with nothing changed on this side: a partner withdraws a protocol version, a provider moves the endpoint behind a hostname, a renewed certificate arrives on a different chain. Take the period's changes at the far ends from the sources that announce them — partner and provider notices, deprecation schedules, renewal dates — and re-check what each affected route now achieves, rather than carrying last period's recorded value forward. A route that fell back and kept working is the case this task exists to catch, because nothing failed and no alert was raised; record each one as open against the owner who must close it.

evidenceHint.en: Period review naming each far-end change taken into account, the routes it touched, what those routes now achieve when they connect, and any still carrying data at a reduced setting with its owner.

templates.title: Removal, transfer and disposition of systems
templates.description: Implements PR.DS-P3: Systems/products/services and associated data are formally managed throughout removal, transfers, and disposition.
templates.objective: To ensure nothing passes out of the organisation's hands by retirement, return, lease end, divestment or tenancy closure until its data has been dealt with and the proof has come back.
templates.successCriteria:
Every ending that actually occurs is listed with the equipment and hosted services it covers and who may sign an item out of use.
By class of system the procedure states what happens to the data before release, who performs and confirms it, and what is kept as proof.
Each item released in the period carries its erasure record, destruction certificate or receiving party's acceptance.
Items without proof stay open against a named owner and a date, not closed on the assumption the process ran.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the list of ending types in scope with the equipment classes and hosted services each covers and the release authority named for it.
Collect the procedure stating, by class of system, what happens to data before release and who performs and confirms it.
Export the period log of items released, the route each left by and the proof returned against it.
Gather erasure records, carriers' destruction certificates and receiving parties' written acceptances.

Analysis:
Reconcile the count of items handed to each carrier against the count certified back to the organisation.
Check items marked gone in the register against what is still racked, still leased or still held in a provider tenancy.
Confirm the person who signed each item out of use was the release authority named for that ending type.
Establish whether endings that happen in practice, such as warranty returns and divestments, appear in the scope at all.

Output:
Period account setting each released item beside the proof received for it.
Schedule of lines still without proof, each carrying an owner and a date.
Gap list of ending types occurring in practice but missing from the scope.

title.en: Identify the systems approaching retirement or handover and who may release them

description.en: Assets rarely end the way a plan imagines: a laptop goes back under warranty, a server comes off a lease, a database moves with a divested team, a hosted tenancy is closed while the provider still holds the volume. Name every such ending that actually occurs here, say which classes of equipment and which hosted services each one applies to, and name the person entitled to sign an item out of use. An ending nobody listed is the one that carries data out of the organisation with nothing recorded about what was done to it first.

evidenceHint.en: List of ending types in scope, the classes of equipment and hosted service each covers, and the person named as release authority for each.

title.en: Record what happens to data when a system is removed, transferred or disposed of

description.en: By class of system, state what must happen to the data it holds before it leaves the organisation's control, who performs that, who confirms it was done, and what is retained as proof. Include systems handed to another party and systems that leave with a person.

title.en: Account for every asset released this period against the confirmations received

description.en: Take the items recorded as released since the last pass and set beside each one the proof returned for it: an erasure record, a destruction certificate from the carrier, or the receiving party's written acceptance of what it now holds. The gaps this catches are the machine marked gone in the register while its disk is still racked, and the batch of twenty collected by a contractor who certified seventeen. Anything still without proof stays open against a named owner and a date, rather than being closed on the assumption that the process ran.

evidenceHint.en: Period log naming each item that left, the route it left by, the proof returned for it, and the lines still open with their owner and date.

templates.title: Capacity for availability
templates.description: Implements PR.DS-P4: Adequate capacity to ensure availability is maintained.
templates.objective: To ensure a service people depend on keeps margin above the limit that will bind it first, and that the organisation learns it is running short before anyone is turned away.
templates.successCriteria:
For every service whose loss would affect individuals, the capacity it needs, how a shortfall becomes known and who is told are recorded.
Services where nobody would learn until failure are recorded with a named owner rather than left off.
Readings come from the busiest period observed and name the limit that bound first, the amount consumed and the margin left.
Where observed demand has overtaken the figure a service was sized for, an exhaustion date is recalculated at the observed rate of growth.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the per-service record of required capacity, the signal by which a shortfall becomes known and the person told.
Collect peak consumption readings dated to the busiest period each service actually saw.
Retrieve the ceilings in force, connection pools, licence seat counts, per-minute quotas and contracted throughput as well as disk and memory.
Gather the demand figure recorded for each service when it was sized.

Analysis:
Check readings are drawn from the peak rather than a monthly average, which hides an hour spent above the ceiling.
Determine which ceiling bound first for each service and how much was left over against it.
Set observed demand beside the sized figure and recalculate the exhaustion date wherever the real number has overtaken the assumption.
Separate growth arriving from a new use from more of the old one, since a trend drawn on last year's shape will not show it.

Output:
Per-service headroom statement naming the binding limit, the amount used against it and the margin that remained.
Recalculated exhaustion dates for services whose demand has overtaken their sizing.
List of services measured too coarsely to see a peak, each with the owner named against it.

title.en: Record the capacity each service needs and how a shortfall becomes known

description.en: For every service whose unavailability would affect individuals, record the capacity it requires to serve them, how the organisation learns it is running short, and who is told when that happens. Record services where nobody would learn until it failed, and name the owner.

title.en: Measure peak consumption against each service's ceiling and record the headroom left

description.en: Take the reading from the busiest period the service actually saw rather than a monthly average, because a service sitting at a third of its ceiling all month can still spend an hour above it and turn people away. For each service record what was consumed at that peak, the ceiling that bound first, and how much was left over — and expect the binding ceiling to be an unglamorous one, since a connection pool, a licence seat count, a per-minute quota or a contracted throughput usually runs out well before disk or memory does. Where nothing records consumption at a resolution fine enough to see the peak, enter that as the finding and name the owner, because an unmeasured service is not a service with headroom.

evidenceHint.en: Per-service reading dated to the busiest period observed, naming the limit that bound first, the amount used against it, and the margin that remained.

title.en: Compare the demand each service actually saw against the figure its plan assumed

description.en: A capacity figure is only as good as the demand it was sized for, and nothing turns red when that assumption quietly stops holding — the service keeps serving while the margin it was built with disappears underneath it. Set the demand observed over the period beside the figure recorded when the service was sized, and wherever the real number has overtaken the assumed one, work out at the observed rate of growth the date the remaining headroom is gone. Pay particular attention to growth that arrived from a new use rather than more of the old one, since a trend drawn from last year's shape will not show it.

evidenceHint.en: Period comparison setting observed demand beside the sized figure for each service, with a recalculated exhaustion date wherever the real number has overtaken the assumed one.
