templates.title: Protections against data leaks
templates.description: Implements PR.DS-P5: Protections against data leaks are implemented.
templates.objective: To ensure data leaves only by a departure somebody agreed to, and that each remaining way out is limited, owned and shown by trial to stop what it claims to stop.
templates.successCriteria:
The scope names the categories whose unsanctioned departure counts as a leak, the agreements making one legitimate, and each category's owner.
Extracts, aggregates and reports are in scope beside the source records they carry outward.
Every way out is enumerated with what limits it and who may authorise an exception, and one with no limit is recorded against its owner.
A marked sample sent down a route is blocked or allowed with an alert raised, and a route not safely exercisable is recorded untested, not passed.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the scope statement listing the categories in scope, the agreements legitimising a departure and the owner named for each.
Collect the enumeration of ways out, onward transfers, exports, correspondence, portable devices and third-party services, with the limit recorded on each.
Retrieve the exception authorisations granted during the period and who granted them.
Gather the test record naming each route exercised, the date, the marked sample used and what happened to it.

Analysis:
Check the categories were taken from the processing inventory with their derived forms, not only the source records.
Establish for each exercised route whether the sample was blocked, allowed, or allowed with nobody alerted.
Compare routes exercised against routes enumerated, the quiet ones included, such as a personal mail client, a file sync client or a support tool able to dump a table.
Confirm a route left unexercised was recorded as an unknown with a reason rather than carried as a success.

Output:
Test record of routes exercised, the outcome of each and the alert it raised.
List of ways out standing with no limit, naming the owner who carries each.
Statement of untested routes with the reason each could not be exercised safely.

title.en: Name the data whose unsanctioned departure would count as a leak

description.en: Egress limits hold nothing in until the organisation has said which data they exist to protect and which departures it has already agreed to — the same record sent under a signed arrangement is legitimate, while a copy of it reaching the same destination by any other means is not. Take the categories from the processing inventory and include the derived forms as well: an extract, an aggregate or a report carries the original outward and is the form most often released without anyone calling it a disclosure. Name the accountable owner of each category, so a route later found open has someone to answer for what sits on it.

evidenceHint.en: Scope statement listing the categories in scope, the agreements that make a departure legitimate, and the named owner of each category.

title.en: Record what limits data leaving the organisation by each available route

description.en: Enumerate the routes by which data could leave — onward transfers, exports, correspondence, portable devices, third-party services — and record what limits each one and who may authorise an exception. Where a route has no limit at all, record it and name the owner who carries it.

title.en: Attempt an export the stated limits should stop and record what got through

description.en: A limit written down and a limit that actually fires are different things, and the difference only shows when something tries to leave. Work from the recorded routes, including the quiet ones — a personal mail client, a file sync client, a support tool that can dump a table — push a marked, harmless sample down each, and note whether it was blocked, allowed, or allowed with nobody alerted. Where a route cannot be exercised safely, write that down rather than a pass: an untested route is an unknown, not a success, and treating it as one is how the gap survives the next check too.

evidenceHint.en: Test record naming each route exercised, the date, the sample used, whether it was blocked or allowed, and the routes left untested with the reason.

templates.title: Integrity of software, firmware and information
templates.description: Implements PR.DS-P6: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify software, firmware, and information integrity.
templates.objective: To ensure that any unauthorised alteration to deployed software, firmware images and stored record sets is detected by comparison against a protected authentic reference.
templates.successCriteria:
Every artefact and record set in scope has a named authentic reference, and those with none are recorded as such rather than left blank.
Reference digests are held where the accounts able to change the artefact cannot rewrite them.
Each protected artefact is compared against its reference at a defined point in its use, and both expected and observed results are retained.
Assets left unverified in a period appear in the check record with a reason, not absent from it.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the scoping list of software builds, firmware images and record sets whose alteration must be detectable.
Obtain the digest register giving each artefact's reference value, where that value is held and the point of use where comparison runs.
Collect the integrity check records for the period, showing expected and observed results per asset.
Request the list of accounts and keys able to rewrite a stored reference value.
Retrieve the scoping entries marked as having no authentic reference available.

Analysis:
Trace a sample of deployed builds and firmware images back to the scoping list to judge whether the population is complete.
Recompute the digest of a sampled artefact and compare it with the value held in the register.
Determine whether the accounts that can modify an artefact are excluded from those that can rewrite its reference value.
Compare the check records against the scoped population to identify assets that went unverified, and weigh the reasons recorded.
Follow any mismatch reported during the period through to its disposition.

Output:
A reconciliation of the scoped artefact population against the digest register.
Recomputation results for the sampled artefacts, with any divergence from the recorded reference.
A statement of which scoped assets were verified in the period and which were not.
A list of accounts holding write access to reference values set beside their access to the artefacts themselves.

title.en: Choose the software, firmware and records whose alteration must be detectable

description.en: List the code, firmware images, configuration files and record sets where a silent change would matter — those that decide how processing runs, and those that stand as the account of what was done to a person's data. For each one, state what its authentic version is judged against: a publisher's signature, a digest taken when it was built, or a sequence chained across the records. Items with nothing trustworthy to compare against — an unsigned supplier binary, a log any administrator can rewrite — belong on the list marked that way, because they are precisely the ones a check will pass without noticing anything.

evidenceHint.en: Scoping list naming each artefact and record set in scope, the authentic reference each is judged against, and the entries marked as having none.

title.en: Generate the authentic digest for each build, firmware image and record set

description.en: Produce the reference value where the artefact is made — at build, at packaging, at the moment a record is committed — and hold it under a key or store the same people and processes cannot also rewrite. A digest recomputed from the file at checking time, or filed beside the file it describes, agrees with any alteration applied to both and will never report one. Fix where the comparison happens — before installation, on load, or when a record is relied on — and what follows a mismatch, since one that only adds a log line leaves the altered software running.

evidenceHint.en: Digest register showing each artefact covered, where its reference value is held, which account or key can rewrite it, and the point in use where the comparison runs.

title.en: Verify the integrity of software, information and hardware and record what was found

description.en: Carry out the checks the organisation relies on to confirm that software, firmware, held information and hardware are as they should be, and record for each what was verified, what the check expects and what it actually found. Record the assets that could not be checked and why.

evidenceHint.en: Check record naming each asset verified, the date, the expected result, the observed result, and the assets left unverified with the reason.

templates.title: Separation of development, test and production
templates.description: Implements PR.DS-P7: The development and testing environment(s) are separate from the production environment.
templates.objective: To ensure that development and test instances cannot reach production systems or hold records belonging to real people, and that the boundary is written down and testable.
templates.successCriteria:
Each system's environment list marks the live instance and states the separation test the others must pass.
Shared services, credentials and data copies joining a test instance to production have been severed, or remain under a named acceptance.
Searches of development and test environments for real people's identifiers return no records, or only records whose disposal is recorded.
Each environment examined retains the date, the identifiers searched for and the hits found.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the environment list for each system, showing the instance marked live and the written separation test.
Collect the per-environment record of shared services, credentials and data copies found, with the action taken on each.
Obtain the named acceptances covering any dependency still shared with production.
Gather the query results from searches of development and test environments for identifiers belonging to real people.
Request the disposal records for live records found outside production.

Analysis:
Apply the written separation test to a sampled non-production instance and judge whether it passes.
Attempt to authenticate to a production service using a credential drawn from a test environment.
Compare the shared-item record against the instance's current connection and configuration state to confirm the severance was made.
Re-run the identifier search independently in one development environment and compare the hits with those reported.
Judge whether each remaining shared dependency carries an acceptance from someone empowered to give it.

Output:
A per-system statement of whether each non-production instance meets the declared separation test.
The result of the credential reuse attempt made against production.
A list of dependencies still shared with production and the acceptance covering each.
Independent search results for live personal records in non-production environments, with the disposal status of each hit.

title.en: Settle what makes an environment separate from production, and list each one

description.en: Separation is asserted far more often than it is defined: two environments can carry different names and still share a database cluster, an identity provider, a message broker or one set of keys. For each system, set out which environments exist - development, test, staging, demonstration, training, a developer's own laptop - which of them is production, and which of infrastructure, network route, credentials and data any pair is forbidden to hold in common. An environment nobody thought to name is the one that turns out to hold live records.

evidenceHint.en: Environment list per system marking the live instance, with the written separation test the other instances are held to.

title.en: Sever the services, credentials and data copies that still join test to production

description.en: Environments drift back together through the parts nobody re-pointed: a staging system authenticating against the live directory, a test job writing to a production queue, an API key that works in both, a nightly restore of the live database into development. Work through each pair on the environment list and either give the lower side its own instance of the shared item, or name who accepted the sharing and what makes it unsplittable. Where production data has already been copied down, the damage is done at the moment the restore lands - supply the lower environments with manufactured records instead, or transform the extract before it is written, rather than masking it once it sits there.

evidenceHint.en: Per-environment list of shared items found, the action taken on each, and the named acceptance for any that remain shared.

title.en: Search each test and development environment for records belonging to real people

description.en: Do not re-read the environment list; go into the lower environments and query for values only a live person could produce - a deliverable mailbox, a real employee number, an address that geocodes. Concentrate on the environments refreshed, rebuilt or stood up for a demonstration since the last pass, and on any a team raised outside the standard build, because that is where a live copy lands. A hit is two findings at once: the separation failed, and the organisation has been holding personal data in a store its inventory never listed, so it belongs in that inventory until it is destroyed.

evidenceHint.en: Query results per environment examined, the identifiers searched for, the date, the hits found, and how each was disposed of or accepted.

templates.title: Integrity of hardware
templates.description: Implements PR.DS-P8: Integrity checking mechanisms are used to verify hardware integrity.
templates.objective: To ensure that substitution of or tampering with a device's physical components is detected when it is received or returned from repair, before the unit is put into service.
templates.successCriteria:
Each device carries a seal and a reference sheet giving its chassis and internal part identifiers as fitted, with the date and the person who applied them.
Every unit received or returned from repair is inspected against that reference sheet before entering service, and the inspection is dated.
A component deliberately substituted into a spare unit is stopped by the receiving inspection.
Devices placed into service without inspection are counted, not assumed to be none.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the per-unit reference sheets giving seal numbers, chassis identifiers and internal part identifiers as fitted.
Collect the dated inspection entries for units received or returned from repair during the period.
Obtain the record of the planted-hardware test, naming what was altered and who handled it.
Request the tally of devices placed into service without a receiving inspection.
Gather the disposition records for units held back after inspection.

Analysis:
Open a sampled unit and compare its seal number and internal part identifiers against its reference sheet.
Match receipt and repair-return events for the period against the inspection entries to find units that bypassed the check.
Determine from the planted-hardware record whether the substitution was stopped, by whom, and how long it took.
Follow each held unit's disposition to confirm it did not re-enter service unresolved.
Consider whether the reference sheets were written at the time of fitting rather than reconstructed afterwards.

Output:
Comparison results for the physically inspected units against their reference sheets.
A reconciliation of receipt and repair-return events against inspection entries.
The outcome of the planted-hardware test with the elapsed time to detection.
A count of devices entering service unchecked, alongside the disposition of units held back.

title.en: Seal each device and register the serials a substitution would have to match

description.en: Fit a tamper-evident measure to every device that holds or processes personal data — chassis seals, sealed transit packaging, a covered port — and write down what intact looks like: the seal identifiers, the chassis serial, and the serials of the internal parts a later inspection can read back. An asset tag is the one marking an interdictor can simply move to another box, so the reference has to be built from marks taken off the hardware itself and held in a store the device cannot write to. Without that reference a replaced drive or a swapped mainboard looks exactly like the unit that was bought, and nothing further down the chain will ever raise it.

evidenceHint.en: Per-unit reference sheet giving seal numbers, chassis and internal part identifiers as fitted, the date, and the person who applied them.

title.en: Inspect the seals and internal parts of every unit received or returned from repair

description.en: Do the physical check at the points where custody left the organisation: a delivery from a supplier or reseller, a machine coming back from a repair bench, a laptop returning from travel that warranted the precaution. Compare the unit in hand against its reference — seals unbroken and bearing the same numbers, internal parts answering with the serials recorded when they were fitted — and hold back anything that disagrees before it is powered onto the network. A maintenance log proves the repair was authorised and says nothing about whether the box that came back is the box that went out; that gap is what this check exists to close.

evidenceHint.en: Dated inspection entries per unit naming the occasion, the seal state found, the parts compared against the reference, and the disposition of anything held back.

title.en: Swap a component into a spare unit and route it through the receiving inspection

description.en: An inspection that has never stopped anything may be working or may be a signature on a form, and the pass record cannot tell those two apart. Take a machine from the spare pool, fit an internal part whose serial does not match its reference, break and re-apply a seal, then send it down the same receipt path a real delivery follows and see whether the person on that path halts it without having been warned. Count, alongside the planted machine, the devices that entered service in the period with no inspection recorded at all, because the units nobody looked at are the population a pass rate hides.

evidenceHint.en: Outcome of the planted-hardware test — what was altered, who handled it, whether it was stopped and how quickly — plus the tally of devices put into service unchecked.

templates.title: Maintenance and repair with approved tools
templates.description: Implements PR.MA-P1: Maintenance and repair of organizational assets are performed and logged, with approved and controlled tools.
templates.objective: To ensure that maintenance on organisational assets uses only approved tools drawn from a controlled store, and that every job is logged with the asset, the person and the tools used.
templates.successCriteria:
Every asset requiring controlled maintenance is named, together with the tools approved for work on it.
Each tool drawn for a job is checked back in, examined on return, and its custody entry closed.
A contractor-supplied device is admitted to a job only against a recorded approval.
Maintenance log entries carry the asset, date, person and tools used, with an approval reference where the work was performed remotely.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the register of assets requiring controlled maintenance and the tool list approved for each.
Collect the tool custody register for the period, showing items drawn, holders, return dates and examination results.
Obtain the maintenance log entries recording asset, date, person and tools used.
Request the approvals held for contractor-supplied devices admitted to the estate.
Gather the organisation's own review record naming the log entries it checked against the approvals.

Analysis:
Select jobs from the maintenance log and trace each tool used back to the approved list for that asset.
Match tool issues in the custody register to their returns and examinations, identifying items still outstanding.
Check whether any job was performed on an asset the register does not list as requiring controlled maintenance.
Verify that each contractor device appearing in a job record has an approval predating its use.
Test whether the organisation's own review surfaced the exceptions your sample found.

Output:
A sample of maintenance jobs with the approval status of every tool used on each.
An outstanding-tool list drawn from custody entries never closed.
A list of jobs run outside the approved tool list or against unregistered assets.
An assessment of the internal review's coverage measured against the exceptions identified.

title.en: Record which assets need controlled maintenance and the tools approved for it

description.en: List the assets that hold or process data whose maintenance must be controlled, and record for each which tools may be used on it and who approves adding a tool to that list. Attach the asset and tool lists together, since a log is later checked against both.

title.en: Issue maintenance tools from a controlled store and check each one back in after the job

description.en: An approved list only governs the kit the organisation owns; the diagnostic laptop a contractor's engineer carries through the door has been inside other customers' equipment and leaves with whatever it copied off yours. Draw every tool against a named job and a named holder, owned or brought in, and examine it on return before it is available for the next asset. Where a repair needs something that is not on the list, the arrangement has to say who may approve it before the work starts, or the list will be amended after the fact to match whatever was used.

evidenceHint.en: Tool custody register listing, per job, the item drawn, who held it, the date returned, the examination result, and any contractor-supplied device admitted with its approval.

title.en: Log each maintenance and repair with the asset, the person and the tools used

description.en: For every maintenance or repair carried out, record the asset, the date, the person who performed it, the tools used and, where the work was done from outside the premises, the approval that permitted it. Record work performed by another party in the same log rather than in that party's own records only.

evidenceHint.en: Maintenance log entries showing the asset, date, person, tools used and, for work performed remotely, the approval reference.

title.en: Check the maintenance log against the approvals and the approved tool list

description.en: Take the logged work since the last check and confirm each remote session had an approval that covered it and each tool used appears on the approved list. Record every exception, whether the asset involved holds data, and what was done about it.

evidenceHint.en: Review record naming the log entries checked and each session or tool found outside the approvals, with the action taken.

templates.title: Remote maintenance
templates.description: Implements PR.MA-P2: Remote maintenance of organizational assets is approved, logged, and performed in a manner that prevents unauthorized access.
templates.objective: To ensure that maintenance reaching an asset from outside the premises is approved in advance, confined to the fault it was opened for, and withdrawn once that work ends.
templates.successCriteria:
Every remote service pathway is recorded with the external party entitled to use it and the interface the connection lands on.
Each pathway on the schedule traces back to the contract clause or device setting that established it.
No remote session runs without a fault ticket naming the work and an approver recorded before the connection opened.
Access is withdrawn once the fix completes, and any session approved after it began carries a retrospective sign-off.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the schedule of remote service pathways with the external party, the interface and the originating contract clause or device setting for each.
Collect the written rule defining how maintenance performed from outside the premises is approved and bounded.
Obtain the session records for the period paired with the fault tickets they were opened for.
Request the connection logs from the interfaces named on the schedule.
Gather the retrospective sign-offs for sessions approved after they began.

Analysis:
Compare the connection logs against the pathway schedule to find remote access arriving by a route the schedule does not name.
Trace a sample of sessions to their fault tickets and confirm the approver was recorded before the connection opened.
Measure the interval between the recorded fix and the withdrawal of access for each sampled session.
Establish whether any external party holds standing access rather than access granted per fault.
Follow each scheduled pathway back to the contract clause or device setting claimed as its origin.

Output:
A reconciliation of observed remote connections against the scheduled pathways.
A sample of sessions showing ticket, approver and the time access was withdrawn.
A list of sessions that opened without prior approval, with the retrospective sign-off held for each.
A statement of which external parties hold access outside the per-fault model.

title.en: List the assets an outside engineer can service without a site visit

description.en: A remote service pathway usually arrives with the equipment rather than being asked for: a management interface the manufacturer enables at installation, a call-home agent inside an appliance, a standing jump host named in a support contract. Read the maintenance and support agreements alongside the devices themselves to name, per asset, the external party entitled to service it that way and the interface they arrive on. An asset missing from this list is serviced under no approval at all, because a procedure can only bind the sessions it knows to expect.

evidenceHint.en: Per-asset schedule of remote service pathways giving the external party entitled to each, the interface it lands on, and the contract clause or device setting it was traced from.

title.en: Define how maintenance performed from outside the premises is approved and bounded

description.en: State who approves a maintenance session conducted from elsewhere, what the person performing it is permitted to reach, what prevents them reaching more, and what must be recorded about the session while it runs. Include what happens when a session must proceed before approval and how it is brought back into the record.

title.en: Bind each remote repair session to its fault ticket and end it with the fix

description.en: The failure here is not an unapproved session but an approved one that never closed: the supplier's account stays enabled, the tunnel stays up, and what was granted for one fault becomes a standing way in. Open the session against a named fault, allow the access to live only while that fault is open, and withdraw it when the work is signed off rather than at the next review. Where a session had to start before approval because the asset was down, capture the retrospective sign-off against the same ticket.

evidenceHint.en: Session records for the period pairing each connection with the fault it was opened for, the approver, the time it was withdrawn, and any retrospective sign-off.

templates.title: Removable media
templates.description: Implements PR.PT-P1: Removable media is protected and its use restricted according to policy.
templates.objective: To ensure that data leaves the estate on removable media only on devices the organisation issued and protected, carrying only content the policy permits on them.
templates.successCriteria:
The permitted media types are stated together with the data categories that may be written to them.
Every issued device appears in the stock register with its serial, its holder and the protection applied to it.
Endpoints refuse a device absent from the issued stock, and the machines carrying that configuration are known.
Each removable-media exception in force has been re-examined against its justification, with the decision and date recorded.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the statement of permitted removable media types and the data categories allowed on each.
Collect the stock register listing issued devices, serials, holders and the protection applied.
Obtain the endpoint configuration that rejects an unlisted device, with the list of machines it reached.
Request the exception list showing each holder, the justification, the decision taken and the date.
Gather the endpoint records of removable device connection attempts for the period.

Analysis:
Insert an unissued device into a sampled endpoint and observe whether it is refused.
Compare the machines covered by the rejecting configuration against the full endpoint inventory to size the uncovered remainder.
Confirm on a sampled issued device that the protection recorded in the stock register is actually in force.
Review the connection records for devices accepted that do not appear on the stock register.
Weigh whether each standing exception was re-justified at its review rather than rolled forward unexamined.

Output:
The result of the unissued-device insertion test on the sampled endpoints.
A coverage figure for the rejecting configuration against the endpoint inventory.
Verification results for the protection claimed on the sampled issued devices.
A list of exceptions with the decision reached at the most recent review of each.

title.en: Record which removable media are permitted and what may be placed on them

description.en: State the classes of removable media that may be used, on which systems, what data may be placed on them, and who may authorise an exception; where none is permitted, record that as the position. Attach the resulting statement and name who holds each exception granted so far.

title.en: Issue encrypted media from controlled stock and have the estate refuse everything else

description.en: Hold the permitted devices as stock the organisation owns, apply the protection before an item is handed over, and record which item went to whom. Then configure the machines that accept a device so one drawn from anywhere else is refused, because a rule written down but never pushed to an endpoint is enforced only by the honesty of whoever is standing at the machine, and a drive somebody bought themselves leaves no trace it ever held anything. Apply the protection to the item rather than to the machine that writes to it, or a copy made on the next computer is plain. Name the machines the configuration could not reach - kiosks, instrument controllers, equipment at another party's site - and who carries each.

evidenceHint.en: Stock register naming each device, its serial, its holder and the protection applied, with the endpoint configuration that rejects an unlisted one and the list of machines it reached.

title.en: Review each granted removable-media exception and decide whether it stands

description.en: List the exceptions in force, confirm the need that justified each still exists, and record the decision to continue, narrow or withdraw it. Record the holder of every exception withdrawn and how they were told.

evidenceHint.en: Review list naming each exception in force, its holder, the justification checked, the decision taken and the date.

templates.title: Least functionality in deployed systems
templates.description: Implements PR.PT-P2: The principle of least functionality is incorporated by configuring systems to provide only essential capabilities.
templates.objective: To ensure that a deployed system offers only the capabilities its role requires, and that anything left enabled beyond that is justified or accepted by a named person.
templates.successCriteria:
Every platform kind in service has a defined reading that shows its enabled capabilities, the tool or query producing it, and a named taker.
Platform kinds with no direct reading available carry an agreed substitute rather than being omitted from scope.
Each capability a deployed system offers stands against a recorded need for it.
Capabilities found unnecessary have been removed on a recorded date, or remain under a named acceptance.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the scoping note listing every platform kind in service, the reading defined for each and its named taker.
Collect the readings taken from live instances, together with the tool or query output behind them.
Obtain the per-system record of offered capabilities set against the need claimed for each.
Request the removal record showing capabilities disabled, the system affected and the date.
Gather the acceptances covering non-essential capabilities still enabled.

Analysis:
Take the defined reading independently from a live instance of a sampled platform kind and compare it with the recorded one.
Identify platform kinds present in the estate but absent from the scoping note.
Examine the substitutes agreed where no direct reading exists and judge whether they reveal enabled capability at all.
Trace capabilities marked as removed to the live system state to confirm they are in fact disabled.
Judge whether the need stated for a retained capability describes a function of that system's role.

Output:
A comparison of independently taken readings against those held on record.
A list of platform kinds in service with no defined reading or an inadequate substitute.
Confirmation status for each capability recorded as removed.
An inventory of enabled non-essential capabilities with the acceptance held for each.

title.en: Pin each platform kind in service to the reading that shows its enabled capabilities

description.en: A capability is not the same object on a host operating system, a network appliance, a database engine, a container image and a tenanted cloud service: one shows installed packages and listening services, another a licensed feature set, another loaded extensions and grants, another a subscription tier the tenant cannot switch off. For every platform kind actually in service, name the reading that will be taken from a live instance to stand as its capability list, and who is able to take it. Where a platform admits no such reading because the provider decides what is enabled, say that now and name what is accepted in its place, or the enumeration will pass over it in silence. Readings chosen ad hoc per instance yield findings that cannot be set against a baseline or carried through to a removal decision.

evidenceHint.en: Scoping note listing every platform kind in service, the reading to be taken from a live instance of each, the tool or query that produces it, the named taker, and the substitute agreed where no direct reading exists.

title.en: Record the capabilities every deployed system offers against the need for them

description.en: Name the list of deployed systems this is worked from and state what it covers and what it leaves out, so the count is checkable rather than assumed. For every system on that list, record the functions, services and interfaces it actually offers, mark which are essential to its purpose and which are not, and name an owner for each that is not; where several systems are deployed from one baseline, record them as a class and name its members, so each finding still lands on a named system. Compare what each offers against the baseline recorded for its class and record where the deployed system has drifted from it, together with any system on the list the enumeration could not reach and why.

title.en: Remove or account for each enabled capability found unnecessary

description.en: For every capability marked non-essential on a deployed system, either remove it and record what was removed and when, or record why it must remain and who accepted its remaining. Record the removals that were attempted and could not be completed.

evidenceHint.en: Per-system record showing each non-essential capability, the action taken, the date, and the named acceptance for any that remain.

templates.title: Communications and control networks
templates.description: Implements PR.PT-P3: Communications and control networks are protected.
templates.objective: To ensure that a party positioned on a network path cannot issue, alter or reuse instructions that the systems at the far end will act upon.
templates.successCriteria:
Each network and link is graded by the instructions an attacker astride it could issue, and the party operating that stretch is named.
Every path carrying communications or control traffic has the protection applied to it recorded.
An instruction captured from a path and resubmitted is not acted on by the receiving system.
Paths that could not be exercised in the replay test are listed with the reason rather than omitted from the result.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the graded list of networks and links with the commands an intruder on each could issue and the operating party.
Collect the record of protection applied to each path carrying communications or control traffic.
Obtain the replay test record naming each path exercised and the instruction resubmitted.
Request the far-end responses observed during that test.
Gather the list of paths that could not be exercised, with the reason given for each.

Analysis:
Compare the graded list against the network topology to find links carrying control traffic that were never graded.
Capture and resubmit an instruction on a path reported as refusing replay, and observe how the far end responds.
Examine whether the protection recorded for a path actually defends against the command its grading anticipates.
Weigh the reasons given for unexercised paths and judge how much control traffic they leave untested.
Establish whether links operated by another party carry protection the organisation can verify rather than only assert.

Output:
A topology reconciliation naming ungraded links that carry control traffic.
The far-end response observed to the independently replayed instruction.
A mapping of each path's recorded protection against the commands its grading anticipates.
A list of untested paths with the control traffic each one carries.

title.en: Grade each network by what an intruder on it could command

description.en: Not every network matters equally here: the ones that carry instructions — console and out-of-band access, orchestration and deployment channels, telemetry that makes something happen at the other end — hand an attacker the estate rather than a copy of a file, and they usually ride the same cabling and the same provider circuits as ordinary traffic. Work through the networks and links the estate actually runs on, including the stretches carried by a telecoms supplier or a hosting provider that cannot be inspected, and grade each by what someone positioned on it could issue or alter, not by how much passes over it. A network nobody designed, such as a flat office segment or a lab left joined to production, belongs on the list at its true grade rather than being left off.

evidenceHint.en: Graded list of the estate's networks and links, each with the instructions an attacker astride it could issue and the party operating the stretch.

title.en: Record the protection applied to the paths carrying communications and control traffic

description.en: For each path over which systems communicate with each other or are managed and controlled, record what protects the traffic on it, who may use the path, and what would follow if the path were interfered with. This covers the management and control channels themselves; the protection of data flows described in the processing map is recorded separately.

title.en: Replay a captured command and see whether the receiving system acts on it

description.en: A path recorded as protected is only an assertion until something tries to abuse it; the common failure is a device that executes any well-formed instruction arriving at its interface, because the designers assumed only trusted equipment could ever put one there. Take a routine instruction from a path already recorded as protected, submit it again unchanged and then altered, and note whether the far end obeys, refuses, or does neither visibly. Include at least one legacy or supplier-operated path, where protection tends to be assumed rather than configured. A path where the attempt cannot be made at all is itself a finding, not an omission.

evidenceHint.en: Test record naming each path exercised, the instruction resubmitted, how the far end responded, and the paths that could not be exercised with the reason.

templates.title: Resilience mechanisms
templates.description: Implements PR.PT-P4: Mechanisms (e.g., failsafe, load balancing, hot swap) are implemented to achieve resilience requirements in normal and adverse situations.
templates.objective: To ensure that each service keeps running through the component losses it was agreed to absorb, and that the arrangements relied on are the ones actually deployed.
templates.successCriteria:
Each service states the single component loss it must ride through and the degradation and duration permitted while it does.
Services able to tolerate no loss at all are recorded as such, each with the owner who agreed that position.
Every component failure seen in the period is matched to the arrangement meant to absorb it and to what actually happened.
Services that saw no failure have had their recorded arrangements re-checked against the live deployment.
templates.testingMethodology:
Evidence:
Obtain the per-service statement of tolerated component loss, permitted degradation and duration, with the owner who agreed it.
Collect the register of arrangements that keep each service available when a part of it fails.
Obtain the period review matching observed component failures to the arrangement expected to cover them.
Request the availability and degradation measurements taken while those failures were in progress.
Gather the re-check records for services that experienced no failure during the period.

Analysis:
Compare the register entry for a sampled service against the configuration actually deployed for it.
Measure the degradation and duration observed during a failure against the limits that service's statement permits.
Identify failures where the register named an arrangement that did not in fact absorb the loss.
Check that services recorded as tolerating no loss carry an owner's agreement rather than an unspoken assumption.
Judge whether the re-checks reached services with no failure history or only those recently changed.

Output:
A per-service comparison of registered arrangements against deployed configuration.
Measured degradation and duration for the period's failures set against the agreed limits.
A list of arrangements that failed to absorb the loss they were recorded against.
Coverage of the no-failure re-check across the service population.

title.en: Set the component losses each service must absorb without stopping

description.en: A resilience mechanism can only be judged against a stated expectation, and most services have never had one written down, so whatever the platform happens to provide quietly becomes the standard. Go service by service and state which single part it is expected to lose and carry on through — an instance, a node, a disk, a broker, an upstream dependency, a whole site — and whether that loss must pass unnoticed or may show as slower work for a stated period. Name the services where the honest answer is that one part takes the whole thing down, because that list is what the rest of this work is aimed at. Where individuals depend on a service, say what they would see while the takeover runs, since a failure nobody notices and one that shows are different promises to them.

evidenceHint.en: Per-service statement of the single part it is expected to ride through, the degradation and duration permitted while it does, and the services recorded as tolerating no loss at all, each with the owner who agreed it.

title.en: Record the arrangements that keep each service available when a part of it fails

description.en: For every service carrying a stated resilience requirement, record what happens when a component of it fails, what takes over, and what an individual relying on the service would experience during the failure. Record the services with no arrangement at all and the owner who accepted that.

title.en: Match each part failure in the period to the mechanism meant to absorb it

description.en: Work from the alerting and incident records for the period rather than from the resilience register, and take every occasion a part of a service failed: what the register said would take over, what actually took over, and how long the gap ran. A standby that came up with work half-finished, or a balancer that went on sending traffic to a dead instance, both count as the mechanism not holding — the service being back by morning is not the test. Where nothing failed at all, check the arrangement against the deployment as it stands today rather than against the register, because redundancy gets dropped quietly during cost work while the record goes on claiming it. What comes out of this is a corrected arrangement or a named owner accepting the gap, not an incident write-up.

evidenceHint.en: Period review listing every failure of a part that was seen, what the register said would cover it, what happened instead, the untouched services re-checked against the live deployment, and the corrections or acceptances that followed.
